org: ETH Zurich (Johannes Schmitt et al.) with a contributor community
note: NeurIPS 2025. The July 2026 paper v2 grew the set from 39 to 77 problems and 14 models, so scores from the two versions do not compare.

name: In-context data exfiltration, visual browser
description: Agents using a visual browser meet attacks that try to exfiltrate data already present in the conversation context. Scored on resisting them.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. The tasks are not public. The ChatGPT Agent card also gives Operator scores on it.

name: In-house CTF suite (Phuong et al. 2024)
aliases: GDM Dangerous Capabilities: Capture the Flag
description: Agents hack 13 simulated servers with vulnerable web apps and services to retrieve a secret flag.
note: Challenges cover web app vulnerabilities, off-the-shelf exploits, databases, Linux privilege escalation and password cracking and spraying. Challenge files without flags or solutions are in the dangerous-capability-evaluations repo. UK AISI inspect_evals ships it as gdm_in_house_ctf, revised seven times to September 2026.

name: INCLUDE
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions from local academic and professional exams in 44 languages that test regional knowledge. Scored by accuracy.
note: INCLUDE-base has 22,637 exam questions in 44 languages. A lite subset of 11,095 questions also exists, and the dataset cards show scores within about a point of the base set. Reports rarely say which set they used.

name: Incorrect behavior rate on disallowed and sensitive content
description: Models answer disallowed prompts and sensitive prompts such as medical advice. Scored on the rate of responses that break policy.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation from the GPT-4 era. Results appear as a chart.

name: IndicGenBench
description: Models summarize, translate, and answer questions across 29 Indic languages using human-translated versions of CrossSum, FLORES, XQuAD, and XorQA. Each task uses its standard metric.
note: Google DeepMind runs it as a Kaggle benchmark (published 2025-12-04, 14 models). It covers 29 Indic languages.

name: Indirect prompt injection, Actor Critic attack
description: An attacker model refines injected email triggers until the agent leaks synthetic private data through a send email call. Reports attack success rate.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation on 500 held-out synthetic conversations.

name: Indirect prompt injection, Beam Search attack
description: An attack appends random tokens to an injected email trigger until the agent leaks synthetic private data. Reports attack success rate.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation on 500 held-out synthetic conversations.

name: Indirect prompt injection, TAP attack
description: A Tree of Attacks with Pruning search writes natural language injections that make the agent leak synthetic private data. Reports attack success rate.
note: In-house Google DeepMind adaptation of TAP to security violations, run on 500 held-out synthetic conversations.

name: IndiVibe
description: Models answer 110 source prompts in chat, STEM, math and coding, translated into 22 Indian languages in native and romanized script. A judge model compares answers pairwise.
note: The judge scores fluency, language and script correctness, usefulness and verbosity. Claude Opus 4 reference answers in English guide the usefulness score. Results are win rates.

name: IndoMMLU
description: Models answer 14,981 multiple-choice questions from Indonesian school and university entrance exams, including nine local languages. Scored by accuracy.

name: IndustryBench
description: Models answer 2,049 Chinese industrial procurement questions grounded in national standards and product records. Answers must respect regulated thresholds and safety clauses.
note: Seven capability dimensions and ten industry categories. About 160 GitHub stars.

name: IneqMath
description: Models solve Olympiad-level inequality problems, recast as two checkable tasks: estimating a tight bound and predicting the relation between two expressions. IMO-level medalists wrote and reviewed the 200 test problems. Five model judges check the final answer and look for toy-case reasoning, logical gaps and numerical shortcuts, and a solution counts only if it passes all five.
note: Scores fall sharply between answer-only and step-wise grading. The makers report judge agreement with humans of F1 0.93 on the dev set. Test answers are held back for the leaderboard, which had 55 entries and was last updated on 2025-08-21. About 60 GitHub stars and 20 Hugging Face upvotes.

name: InferenceEval
description: Agents land real production changes in the xAI inference stack. Hidden GPU unit tests and integration probes grade each patch.
note: In-house xAI evaluation, first reported in the Grok 4.6 card.

name: Infinite Generations (Mistral internal)
description: Models answer challenging long or repetitive prompts from Mistral's internal set. The score is the share of responses that never stop or loop, so lower is better.
note: Mistral reported it in the Mistral Small 3.2 card to show fewer runaway generations than Small 3.1. The prompt set and the detection rule are not published.

name: InfiniteBench/En.MC
description: Models answer 229 multiple choice questions about long fake books with altered entity names, averaging about 184K tokens. Scoring is accuracy.
note: This is one subtask of InfiniteBench, which has 12 tasks in English and Chinese.

name: InfiniteBench/En.QA
description: Models answer free-form questions about novels longer than 100K tokens. Scored by F1 against reference answers.
note: The multiple-choice task on the same novels is infinitebench-en-mc.

name: InFoBench
description: Models follow 500 instructions that are split into 2,250 yes or no requirement questions. A judge answers each question, and the score is the share met.
note: The metric is the Decomposed Requirements Following Ratio (DRFR). GPT-4 is the usual judge.

name: Infographic factuality (Google)
description: Image generation systems produce infographics and an automated rater scores factuality.
note: Nano Banana 2.1 reports an internal infographic factuality score as a fraction.

name: InfographicVQA
description: Models answer about 30,000 questions on about 5,000 infographics that mix text, layout, charts, and graphics. Scoring is ANLS.
org: Computer Vision Center (UAB) and IIIT Hyderabad

name: Information Extraction (ByteDance Seed in-house)
description: Models extract words, sentences or fields from meeting records, legal texts, contracts, product descriptions and knowledge bases.
note: One of six in-house application sets in the Seed1.8 and Seed2.0 model cards. Scoring is a guess.

name: Information Processing (ByteDance Seed in-house)
description: Models analyze large collections of user-generated content, for example summarizing viewpoints and judging overall sentiment.
note: One of six in-house application sets in the Seed1.8 model card. Scoring is a guess.

name: InnovationEval
description: Agents with thousands of GPU hours try to discover an ML technique that matches a recent human paper they have not seen. The score is the share of that paper's gain the agent reaches.
note: First iteration targets Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO). GPT-5.6 Sol reached at most 15% of SDPO gains at equal wall-clock time. Epoch plans to repeat it.

name: Input hallucinations (Anthropic)
description: Models answer 500 prompts that need an unavailable tool and 500 prompts that cite missing context. Score is the non-hallucination rate.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. Reported as two sets with no overall score.

name: InsCtrl (Tencent)
description: Models write text under detailed instructions in a Tencent in-house text creation test. Task and scoring details are not published.
note: Seen in the Hunyuan-A13B-Instruct card. Scoring method is a guess from the task type.

name: Instruction Following (MiniMax in-house)
description: Models follow multi-level instructions collected from user cases where current models fail.
note: In-house MiniMax evaluation built mostly from Hailuo AI user queries in Mandarin. The queries are not public.

name: Instruction Following (safety evaluation)
description: An automated evaluation measures whether the model follows instructions on sensitive prompts while staying within safety policies.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. Model cards and the Gemini 2.5 report give only the change against Gemini 1.5.

name: Instruction hierarchy attacks
description: Models face attacks that try to override higher-priority instructions. Scored as defender success rate averaged per defender query.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Instruction Hierarchy Evaluation
description: Models resolve conflicts between system, developer and user messages, resist tutor jailbreaks, and protect secret phrases and passwords. Scored per sub-evaluation.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Cards report sub-evaluations with no overall number.

name: InstructTTSEval
description: Text-to-speech models follow natural-language style instructions in English and Chinese across acoustic parameter, descriptive style and role-play tasks. Gemini judges each clip.
org: Fudan University (Kexin Huang, Xipeng Qiu and others)
note: The set has 6,000 test cases, 1,000 per task and language, each with reference audio.

name: Instrument reading (Google DeepMind)
description: Models read gauges, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers and thermometers from robot camera images. ER 2 tests 10 instrument types.
note: Introduced with Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 in 2026-04 with Boston Dynamics inspection use cases and generalized in the ER 2 post.

name: Instrumental convergence evals
description: Agents in 7 low-friction tasks can guard goals or acquire optionality against task instructions. Reports the rate of self-serving actions.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: IntelligentBench
description: Image editing models complete 350 free-form edits that need reasoning and world knowledge. GPT-4o scores each output from 0 to 2 against a reference image, normalized to 100.
note: In-house benchmark proposed in the BAGEL paper. Criteria are request fulfillment, visual consistency and knowledge-grounded creativity.

name: Intention Recognition (ByteDance Seed in-house)
description: Models classify intent from dialogues, meeting transcripts, social posts and articles, such as purchase intent in customer service chats.
note: One of six in-house application sets in the Seed1.8 model card. Scoring is a guess.

name: Intentionally taking actions very rarely (Anthropic)
description: Models are told to take a specific action at a target rate such as 1 percent. Resampling measures the observed rate under several randomness settings.
note: Internal replication of Serrano et al. 2026. Settings include a UUID in the prompt, String Seed of Thought and no randomness source.

name: Inter-GPS (Geometry3K)
description: Models solve high school geometry problems that combine a diagram and text from the Geometry3K test set. Scored by accuracy.
org: UCLA and Sun Yat-sen University (Lu et al.)

name: InteractiveBench
description: Multimodal models act as a wearable assistant that sees through a simulated person's eyes and guides that person through household tasks. State-based checks in a BEHAVIOR-1K home score the outcome.
note: 120 multi-turn tasks in six categories, 20 each, built on the InteractiveWorld simulator. 12 frontier models in the first release. Claude Fable 5.1 reached at most 25% on long-horizon categories.

name: InterCode-CTF
description: Agents solve 100 picoCTF capture-the-flag challenges in an interactive Bash and Python environment.
note: Agents work in an interactive Bash and Python environment on picoCTF challenges in coding, cryptography, reverse engineering and vulnerability finding. Google omits challenges that need internet access, leaving 76. UK AISI inspect_evals ships it as gdm_intercode_ctf.

name: Internal adversarially-designed factuality evaluations
description: Models answer adversarial questions in nine categories such as history, math and code. Scored on agreement with human ideal responses.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Results appear as a chart by category.

name: Internal agentic coding evaluation (Anthropic)
description: Agents implement a pull request in an open source codebase from a natural language description. A problem counts as solved when all hidden tests pass.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation based on real pull requests, first reported in the Claude 3.5 Sonnet model card addendum. The tasks are not public.

name: Internal AI research evaluation suite 2
description: Agents perform scaled-down ML and alignment research tasks similar to past Anthropic research projects.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Internal API instruction following (OpenAI)
description: Models answer prompts drawn from real developer use cases that carry instructions on formatting, verbosity and length. OpenAI reports a hard subset.
note: OpenAI introduced it with GPT-4.1 on 2025-04-14 and reported it again in the GPT-5 developer post on 2025-08-07. The grading method is not described, so model-judged is assumed.

name: Internal codebase monitor evasion eval
description: Agents do a real coding task in a snapshot of Google's monorepo while hiding a harmful side task from action and CoT monitors.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation inspired by OAI-repo-sabotage. Uses 18 monitor-validated task pairs.

name: Internal codebase sabotage propensity (Anthropic)
description: Agents in Claude Code write a costly internal classifier they may dislike. Score is the rate of writing a sabotaged classifier.
note: In-house Anthropic scenario. The scenario is not public.

name: Internal computer use safety benchmark (OpenAI)
description: Models complete computer-use tasks while avoiding unsafe actions.
note: OpenAI reports lower-is-better failure rates in the GPT-6 Astra launch comparison.

name: Internal model use survey (Anthropic)
description: Anthropic technical staff estimate productivity uplift from the model and judge whether it could automate a junior ML researcher.
note: Survey of Anthropic staff, not a task set.

name: Internal Research Debugging Evaluation
description: Agents debug difficult problems from OpenAI research work that take researchers hours or days. Scored as mean rubric score.
note: In-house OpenAI AI self-improvement evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Internal vulnerability research
description: Agents find a vulnerability from an entry point, with or without source, then write a working exploit. Based on Google red team exercises.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Into the Unknown
aliases: Into the Unknown (DOE open research benchmark)
description: Agents get a science paper and an unpublished follow-up direction from a DOE national lab scientist, then write the follow-up paper. Rubrics built from the scientist's conditions grade it, plus an integrity check.
org: Prometheus-Eval team with US DOE national laboratories (Seungone Kim et al.)
note: Nine agents wrote 15 follow-ups each. None of the 135 papers met all conditions, and 114 failed the integrity check. 152 HF paper upvotes.

name: IntPhys 2
description: Models watch simulated videos and judge whether each event is physically possible, testing object permanence, immutability, continuity and solidity. Scored by accuracy.
note: Released with V-JEPA 2. The leaderboard scores a held-out split of 344 videos whose answers stay private. The CAIS AI leaderboard also runs it on frontier models.

name: Introductory Sommelier (theory knowledge)
description: Models answer wine theory questions at the introductory sommelier level. Scoring is accuracy.
note: OpenAI ran this as a simulated exam in the GPT-4 Technical Report.

name: Inverse IFEval
description: Models follow 1,012 Chinese and English instructions that conflict with habits learned in fine-tuning, such as writing code without comments. A model judge scores compliance.
org: ByteDance Seed and collaborators (Zhang et al.)
note: Eight challenge types across 23 domains. It is a different test from IFEval.

name: Investment Banking Modeling Tasks (OpenAI)
description: Models build first- to third-year investment banking analyst models, such as three-statement and leveraged buyout models, with formatting and citations. OpenAI grades the outputs internally.
note: OpenAI first reported it for ChatGPT agent on 2025-07-17, as first- to third-year analyst modeling tasks such as three-statement and leveraged buyout models. The GPT-5.2 post called it Investment banking spreadsheet tasks, with GPT-5.2 at 68.4 under both names. The grading method is not described, so model-judged is assumed.

name: Investor's Last Exam
description: Financial agents make equity investment judgments from a frozen set of decision-time evidence. Predictions are scored against later outcomes and professional criteria.
note: 128 GitHub stars at 2026-11-01.

name: IOI (Vals)
description: Agents solve International Olympiad in Informatics problems from 2024 and 2025 in C++. A submission tool modeled on the contest grades up to 50 tries per problem by subtask.
note: Vals archived v1 as saturated after 2026-08-09, with Claude Opus 5 first at 91.67%. Not the same as the almanac's single-year IOI 2025 record.

name: IOI 2025
description: Model solves the 2025 International Olympiad in Informatics tasks. Scored with official subtask points (max 600).
note: Contest problems are public. No single public LLM harness found.

name: IOI v2 (Vals)
description: Agents solve 18 International Olympiad in Informatics problems from 2024, 2025 and 2026 in C++ inside OpenCode. Official tests and graders score the final solution by subtask after the run.
note: Unlike v1 there is no interactive grading tool, and Vals says the two harnesses are not comparable. Score is the mean of three yearly scores. Released between 2026-08-09 and 2026-10-29.

name: iOSWorld
description: Phone agents work in a native iOS simulator across 26 purpose-built apps that share one persistent user's data. Tasks span single apps, multi-app flows and memory or personalization from the user's history.
note: 133 tasks: 27 single-app, 60 multi-app and 46 memory and personalization. Vision-only and vision plus XML settings. Best setup reached 51.9% overall. Apple's iPrefBench builds on it.

name: IPhO 2025
description: Models solve the theory problems of the 2025 International Physics Olympiad. Answers are graded against the official marking scheme.
note: Labs grade it themselves, so scores across labs may use different graders. Seed reports it for Seed2.1 Pro and Deep Think.

name: IPI Bench
description: Agents complete workplace workflows while attackers add misleading records to an emulated company with 11 services. The benchmark pairs six workflow types with harmful injected objectives across 34 tasks. The headline here measures single-query attack success as a percentage, where lower is better.
note: Models run at medium reasoning effort without added defenses. Judges assess task-specific rubrics, and reviewers check every claimed attack success. The report separately gives independent and iterative attack budgets. Clean-workflow cost and total tokens describe runs without attacks. The report dates itself to October 2026.

name: Iris Safety Evaluations
description: Reflection AI's in-house safety suite of single-turn, multi-turn, jailbreak and agentic requests. Reports the share of harmful requests refused or redirected and the share of harmless requests answered.
note: In-house test. Prompts are not public.

name: IrokoBench
description: Models answer human-translated knowledge, math and inference questions in 16 African languages. The parts are AfriMMLU, AfriMGSM and AfriXNLI.
note: lm-evaluation-harness ships the three parts as afrimmlu, afrimgsm and afrixnli.

name: Irregular FrontierCyber and Atomic Challenges
description: Irregular's external suites: FrontierCyber (226 real software/hardware challenges) and Atomic Challenges (22 skill-level tasks).

name: Irrelevant instructions, text-based web browser
description: Agents using a text browser meet synthetic web pages with irrelevant instructions or data exfiltration attempts. Scored on ignoring them.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation built from synthetic examples. The tasks are not public.

name: Irrelevant instructions, visual browser
description: Agents using a visual browser meet irrelevant instructions or data exfiltration attempts on web pages, based on red teaming scenarios. Scored on ignoring them.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. The tasks are not public. The ChatGPT Agent card also gives Operator scores on it.

name: ITBench
description: Agents handle IT automation tasks in Kubernetes environments: site reliability incidents, compliance and security checks, and cloud cost work.
note: Presented as an oral at ICML 2025. IBM and Kaggle added an ITBench leaderboard in 2025-12.

name: ITBench-AA
description: Agents read an offline snapshot of a failing Kubernetes cluster and name the entities that caused the incident, in structured JSON.
note: Launched 2026-05-27 with 59 SRE scenarios from ITBench, 40 of them public. FinOps and CISO tasks are planned. An LLM normalizes entities before matching.

name: Ivo-micro1 ContractBench
description: Models review contracts and return redlines across 350 attorney-written tasks in 35 scenarios and five agreement types. Tasks cover first review and replies to a counterparty.
note: Scores whether models intervene where several attorneys did, plus a surgicality index of targeted inline edits. Attorneys scored 63.5% on surgicality.

name: Jailbreak Augmented Examples
description: Models face publicly known jailbreaks applied to prompts from the standard disallowed content set. Scored as not_unsafe rate.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation built from public jailbreak techniques.

name: JailbreakBench
description: 100 harmful and 100 benign behaviors with a standard jailbreak artifact library. Scored by attack success rate.

name: JEF-Bench
description: Agents read files that embed jailbreak instructions in tool-call returns. Reports attack success rate across 1800 tasks and 50 disallowed use cases.
note: In-house Meta evaluation introduced in the Muse Spark 1.3 report.

name: JevBench
description: Decision models, such as TypeSafe AI's Jev and compatible systems, answer typed decision questions. The board scores accuracy, probability calibration, latency and cost.
note: Maintained independently of TypeSafe AI. Show HN post had 154 points. Related to the Decision Index board.

name: Jigsaw Toxic Comment Classification
description: Models label Wikipedia talk page comments for toxicity types such as threats, insults and identity hate. Labs report F1 or ROC AUC.
org: Jigsaw and Google (Conversation AI), hosted on Kaggle
note: The data comes from a 2017 Kaggle competition. Amazon uses it as a content moderation test for Nova 2 with F1.

name: JMMLU
description: Models answer 7,536 four-way multiple-choice questions in Japanese, from translated MMLU subjects and new Japan-specific subjects. Scored by accuracy.

name: JobBench
description: 130 tasks from 35 occupations workers most want delegated. Agent works through messy reference files, graded by fact-anchored binary rubrics.
note: Framed as an alternative to GDPval's economic-value framing. Vendor-reported scores run higher than the paper's best (45.9%).

name: JointAVBench
description: Models answer questions about videos that cannot be answered from vision or audio alone. Questions cover speech and sound events over several scene spans.
note: The Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash table spells it JoinAVBench.

name: Joke Arena
description: Models write jokes. Pairwise votes determine the published Arena rating.
note: The official API publishes an Arena rating, confidence interval and vote count. Voter identity requires confirmation from the board description.

name: JudgeBench
description: Models act as judges and pick the correct response from hard pairs on knowledge, reasoning, math and coding. The label comes from objective correctness, not human preference.
note: ICLR 2025 paper.

name: Judgemark v2.1
description: The model under test acts as a judge and scores creative writing on several literary criteria. The benchmark measures how well its scores separate stronger writers from weaker ones.
note: v2.1 swapped in stronger writer models to fight saturation and added judge ensembling. Now listed as a legacy board.

name: Judgemark v4
description: The model under test judges fixed creative-writing samples against low and high anchor responses. The score is how well its ratings separate writer models.
note: Each item has a lower anchor scored 2 and an upper anchor scored 9. Scoring uses separability metrics such as omega squared. Release date not stated on the page.

name: K-BrowseComp
description: Web browsing agents answer 400 hard search problems grounded in Korean contexts. A 300-problem Verified subset was built and checked by native speakers.
note: Frontier models scored 30% to 46% on the Verified subset at launch. 56 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: K-Sort Arena
description: Users rank outputs from K image or video generation models at once instead of a pair. Bayesian updates turn the rankings into ratings.
org: Li et al. (UC Berkeley and collaborators)
note: Published at CVPR 2025. It reports 16.3 times faster convergence than Elo. It covers text-to-image and text-to-video.

name: K-Viscuit
description: Models answer multiple-choice visual questions about Korean culture. Questions were written through human and VLM collaboration.
org: Seoul National University and collaborators (ddehun et al.)
note: Published as an arXiv preprint in 2024-06.

name: KAET (Kimi Autonomous Execution Tasks)
description: Agents execute long-horizon tasks that simulate real user requests and enterprise system operations.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Kaggle Game Arena
description: Language models play each other in board, card and word games through a text harness. One leaderboard ranks models across all Game Arena games.
note: Launched with a chess exhibition on 2025-08-04. By 2026-10-19 the suite covered 19 games and 39 models, including Go, checkers, reversi, Dark Hex and Werewolf.

name: Kaleidoscope
description: Vision-language models answer 20,911 multiple choice questions from real exams in 18 languages of 8 families. About 55% of the questions need an image. Accuracy.
note: Questions stay in their original language rather than being translated from English.

name: KAT Claw Bench
description: Agents complete business tool-use tasks from Kuaishou internal agent needs in seven categories, such as office work, content operations, data analysis and monitoring. Automatic checks grade objective outputs, and model and human review grade open deliverables.
note: In-house Claw-style benchmark described in the KAT-Coder-V2.5 tech report.

name: KAT Code Bench
description: Agents turn a natural-language requirement into a patch in a real repository drawn from Kuaishou internal development work. Each task pins its commit, environment and an executable verification entry point across 12 languages.
note: In-house benchmark described in the KAT-Coder-V2.5 tech report. It covers bug fixes, feature work, compatibility and cross-module edits.

name: KBank-MMLU (Upstage)
description: Models answer Korean finance questions in a multiple-choice format. Upstage built the set in house.
note: The technical report lists it as the finance part of the professional domain group, with no further detail.

name: KBL
aliases: Korean Benchmark for Legal Language Understanding
description: Models answer Korean legal knowledge and reasoning tasks and Korean bar exam questions. It has 7 knowledge tasks, 4 reasoning tasks and 2,510 bar exam items.
org: LBox and collaborators (Yeeun Kim et al.)
note: Published at EMNLP 2024 Findings. Lawyers helped build the knowledge and reasoning tasks.

name: Keeping secrets when pressed in simulated scenarios (Anthropic)
description: Models hold confidential information in 39 job scenarios while a simulated counterpart presses for it. Measures leaks in replies and in reasoning.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. Claude Opus 5.5 plays the counterpart for up to 20 turns.

name: KellyBench
description: Agents bet through a simulated 2023 to 24 English Premier League season with historical data. The score is long-term bankroll growth.
note: At launch every tested frontier model lost money. Covered in Latent Space AINews on 2026-04-09.

name: Kernel Bench L3
description: Models write fast GPU kernels for the 50 full model architectures in KernelBench Level 3. Scored on correctness and speedup over PyTorch.
note: This is the hardest of the three original KernelBench levels, which cover single operators, fusions, and full models.

name: KernelBench
description: Replace PyTorch operators with faster custom GPU kernels. Scored on correctness and speedup.
note: KernelBench v0.1 (July 2025) fixed problem sizes and numerics, added randomized tests and a Level 4 of Hugging Face models. The HF dataset tracks v0.1. xAI reports an internal derivative, KernelBenchInternal v1.1.

name: KernelBench (kernelbench.com)
description: Coding agents write GPU kernels for real model workloads, such as fused MoE layers, paged attention and FP8 matrix multiplies. The site groups tasks into suites: Mega (one decode task), CUDA (4 tasks) and Hard (6 tasks). A run counts only if it passes an audit of correctness. Scores are speedup over a baseline or percent of the hardware roofline.
note: The site says it is not affiliated with Stanford's KernelBench. The almanac's Stanford record lists "KernelBench Hard" as an alias, and MiniMax M3's "KernelBench Hard" score may refer to this site's Hard suite instead, so that mapping needs a check. All linked runs are on an RTX PRO 6000. One CUDA result reads above 100% of roofline. About 99 GitHub stars.

name: KernelBenchInternal
description: Agents replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. Scores combine correctness and measured speedup over a TF32 baseline.
note: In-house xAI suite inspired by KernelBench. Version 1.1 uses a harder task split.

name: KernelGen 1P
description: Agents write and optimize GPU kernels under hardware constraints and debug correctness issues. Scored as mean rubric score.
note: In-house OpenAI AI self-improvement evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Kernels task (Anthropic)
description: Agents optimize compute kernels in a performance engineering challenge. Scored by speedup.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Key insight rediscovery on an unpublished ML task (external testing)
aliases: Unpublished machine learning task insight rediscovery
description: Agents work on an unpublished machine learning research task. Testers count how many of five key insights the agent rediscovers.
note: Run by an unnamed external testing partner on a pre-release snapshot. The task is not public.

name: KeyFrame-Compass
description: Video generators must reproduce a given sequence of keyframes while keeping overall video quality. The set has 386 samples over three domains and four keyframe densities.
note: It had 42 Hugging Face paper upvotes and 10 GitHub stars.

name: KGC-Safety (LG)
description: Models answer risky prompts set in Korean social and cultural contexts. A Safe Rate is scored over four domains: universal human values, social safety, Korean sensitivity and future risk.
note: LG introduced it in the K-EXAONE technical report. It is built on LG's K-AUT risk taxonomy, which grew from 226 to 296 risk areas in its second version.

name: KilometerVision
description: Models watch walking-tour videos geolocated over up to 1 km and answer questions on landmarks, routes and map layout, such as distances and loop closures.
note: A new track of the fourth Perception Test Challenge at ECCV 2026, which opened on 2026-06-20. The paper followed on 2026-09-30. A sibling track, KilometerAudio, uses hour-long walking tours with audio.

name: Kimi Chinese in-house open-ended benchmark
description: Models answer held-out Chinese prompts drawn from real user queries. Outputs are compared pairwise against another model to give win, tie and loss rates.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. Access to the data is restricted.

name: Kimi Claw 24/7 Bench
description: Agents work on 17 persistent multi-day professional scenarios through OpenClaw, with 610 checkpoints. The score is the mean pass rate over three runs.
note: In-house: Moonshot never released the tasks.

name: Kimi Code Bench
description: Moonshot in-house coding-agent tasks from internal engineering cases, production incidents and open-source projects across 10+ languages. 80 tasks.
note: Lab-created in-house eval (Moonshot AI). Only Moonshot reports scores. V1 and v2 scores are not comparable. Cyber tasks trigger refusals.

name: Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon
description: Coding agents carry out long multi-step engineering tasks with tools across several engineering domains. Moonshot reports a percentage score.
note: In-house. Moonshot reports it next to Kimi Code Bench 2.0, so it may be a separate long-horizon test rather than a replacement. Scoring method is not described.

name: Kimi Code Bench v2
description: Coding agents complete Moonshot's realistic tasks from internal engineering work, production incidents, and open-source projects in over ten languages.
note: In-house: Moonshot never released the tasks, and only Moonshot reports scores on it.

name: Kimi exploit development suite
description: Agents turn real CVEs into working exploits in 16 user-space tasks and 20 Linux kernel privilege-escalation tasks. Experts verified every task solvable.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation of 36 tasks. The tasks are not public.

name: Kimi Hallu Bench
description: Models answer hard prompts drawn from practical work tasks. Fact-checking agents score the share of claims that are hallucinated.
note: In-house. Moonshot reports a set without tools and a Hard set with tools. Moonshot says the rates are a stress test and not daily error rates.

name: Kimi Promptfoo red-team safety evaluation
description: Promptfoo generates attack prompts for harmful, criminal, misinformation, privacy and security plugins under five strategies. Human reviewers judge the responses.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation built with the open Promptfoo tool. Results are passing rates per plugin and strategy.

name: Kimi vulnerability discovery (Tier 1)
description: Agents search current versions of widely deployed software for new bugs and show that they reproduce. Humans review the findings.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. Results are reported as confirmed findings, not as a score.

name: Kimi Webdev Bench
description: Models build games, 3D scenes and website clones from real prompts. Blind experts compare two outputs and report win, tie and loss rates.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. Kimi K3 is compared only against Claude Opus 4.8.

name: Kimi-ASR Internal Testset
description: Models transcribe speech from two internal Moonshot test subsets. Scored by word error rate, lower is better.
note: In-house Moonshot evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Kimi-ASR Internal Testset Subset 1
description: Models transcribe speech from Moonshot internal subset 1. The score is the published word error rate.
note: One track of Kimi-ASR Internal Testset. The Kimi-ASR Internal Testset record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: Kimi-ASR Internal Testset Subset 2
description: Models transcribe speech from Moonshot internal subset 2. The score is the published word error rate.
note: One track of Kimi-ASR Internal Testset. The Kimi-ASR Internal Testset record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: Kimi-Audio speech conversation evaluation
description: People rate spoken replies on speed, accent and emotion control, empathy and style control. Scored on a 1 to 5 scale and averaged.
note: In-house Moonshot evaluation. The report says Moonshot releases the recorded set, but the Kimi-Audio-Evalkit README lists no such dataset.

name: KINA
description: Models answer 899 knowledge questions across 261 fine-grained disciplines, each with ten lettered options. Scored by accuracy against the key.
note: The paper evaluates 42 models from 13 labs. ByteDance Seed reports it in the Seed2.1 launch.

name: Kitab
description: Models list books by a given author that meet extra constraints, such as publication dates or title words. Scored by precision and constraint satisfaction.

name: KMMLU
description: Models answer 35,030 Korean multiple-choice questions across 45 subjects, collected from original Korean exams. Scoring is accuracy.

name: KMMLU-Hard
description: Models answer about 5,000 Korean multiple-choice questions from KMMLU that most models got wrong, across many expert subjects.
note: A hard subset released with KMMLU. Korean model reports often cite it.

name: KMMLU-Pro
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions taken from Korean National Professional Licensure exams. It tests professional knowledge used in Korean industry.
note: Released in the same paper as KMMLU-Redux. The Hugging Face dataset is gated.

name: KMMLU-Redux
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions from Korean National Technical Qualification exams. The set is rebuilt from KMMLU with erroneous questions removed.
note: Released in the same paper as KMMLU-Pro. Scores are not comparable with the original KMMLU.

name: KMMMU
description: Models answer 3,466 college and exam level questions that combine images with Korean text. Questions come from Korean exam sources, some with several images.
note: A Korean counterpart of MMMU. The dataset repo was created in 2026-02 and the technical report followed in 2026-04.

name: Knowledge Q&A (MiniMax in-house)
description: Models answer knowledge questions drawn from real Hailuo AI user queries.
note: In-house MiniMax evaluation built mostly from Hailuo AI user queries in Mandarin. The queries are not public.

name: KnowMe-Bench
description: Models read long autobiographical narratives and must infer a person's stable motivations and decision principles, not just retrieve facts.
note: 42 HF paper upvotes and about 140 GitHub stars. Aimed at lifelong digital companions.

name: Ko-AIME 2024 (Upstage)
description: Models solve AIME 2024 competition problems translated into Korean. Upstage built the set in house.
note: In-house Upstage evaluation. The tasks are not public. Ko-AIME 2025 is a separate record (ko-aime-upstage).

name: Ko-AIME 2025 (Upstage)
description: Models solve AIME 2025 competition problems in Korean. Upstage built the set in house.
note: The technical report lists it only as an in-house Korean math benchmark. The Korean framing is read from its name.

name: Ko-Arena-Hard v2 (Upstage)
description: Models answer hard user prompts in Korean, judged against a baseline in the style of Arena-Hard v2. Upstage built it in house.
note: Upstage marks it as in-house on the Solar Open 100B card and reports it again for the March 2026 Solar Pro 3 update. Its Korean prompt source is not published.

name: Ko-GDPval
description: Agents complete 170 Korean office tasks from 58 occupations in 11 industries and produce deliverable files. Rubrics grade data, content, structure, quality and format.
note: Upstage built it in house in the style of OpenAI's GDPval, from its OfficeVerse task pipeline.

name: Ko-IFEval (Upstage)
description: Models follow verifiable instructions written in Korean. Upstage adapted IFEval to Korean for the Open Ko-LLM Leaderboard2.
note: In-house Upstage evaluation. The tasks are not public. The Solar Open report calls it an in-house Korean adaptation of IFEval.

name: Ko-LongBench (LG)
description: Models answer questions over long Korean contexts. Tasks cover document QA, story and dialogue history understanding, in-context learning, structured QA and RAG.
note: LG AI Research built it in house and first described it in the EXAONE 4.0 technical report.

name: KoBALT
aliases: Korean Benchmark For Advanced Linguistic Tasks
description: Models answer 700 expert-written multiple-choice questions on 24 Korean linguistic phenomena in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, phonology and morphology.
org: Seoul National University and collaborators (Hyopil Shin et al.)
note: Questions have little n-gram overlap with standard Korean corpora, to limit contamination.

name: KoBEST
aliases: Korean Balanced Evaluation of Significant Tasks
description: Models do five Korean tasks designed by professional linguists: BoolQ, COPA, WiC, HellaSwag and SentiNeg. All data is human-annotated.
org: SK Telecom and collaborators (Kim, Jang et al.)
note: LG's EXAONE 3.0 report (2024-08) uses it with KMMLU as its Korean general benchmarks. lm-evaluation-harness has the tasks.

name: KoMT-Bench
description: Models follow multi-turn instructions in Korean on a translated and culturally adapted version of MT-Bench, reviewed by expert linguists.
note: In-house set released with EXAONE models.

name: Kontext Bench
description: Image editing models get 1,026 image and instruction pairs across local edits, global edits, text editing, style reference and character consistency.
note: Built from 108 base images. Image editing has no own subcategory, so it sits under generation. Scoring method should be checked.

name: KOR-Bench
description: Models read a new rule set and apply it to questions in five task types: operation, logic, cipher, puzzle and counterfactual. Scored by accuracy against an answer key.
org: Multimodal Art Projection (M-A-P) with ByteDance and 01.AI
note: The rules are designed to be independent of domain knowledge. ByteDance Seed reports it in Seed-OSS and Seed 1.6 launch posts.

name: KORA
description: Simulated child users hold 3-turn conversations probing 26 child-specific risks. Judge model rates replies failing, adequate or exemplary.
note: Public leaderboard is KORA V2 (repo tags 2.0.0 to 2.2.0, latest 2026-10-26). V3 changes scenario building and the judge and is in validation, so V2 and V3 scores will not be comparable. Relies on synthetic personas and an AI judge.

name: KORA Apps
description: Simulated children use consumer AI apps end to end, with each app system prompt, filters and safeguards active. Scores cover online, physical and sexual, psycho-social and learning risks.
note: Rates apps, not bare models, in child and adult modes. First board dated 2026-07-26 lists about 20 app entries such as MagicSchool, ChatGPT and SchoolAI.

name: KorMedMCQA
description: Models answer 7,469 multiple-choice questions from Korean licensing exams for doctors, nurses, pharmacists and dentists, held from 2012 to 2024.
org: KAIST and collaborators (Sunjun Kweon et al.)
note: A multimodal follow-up, KorMedMCQA-V, appeared in 2026-02.

name: KRETA
description: Models read and reason over Korean text in images across diverse visual contexts. It is a text-rich visual question answering test for Korean.
note: Published at EMNLP 2025. The leaderboard is a table in the GitHub README.

name: KRIS-Bench
aliases: Knowledge-based Reasoning in Image-editing Systems Benchmark
description: Image editing models follow 1,267 instructions that need factual, conceptual or procedural knowledge across 22 tasks. A GPT-4o judge scores the edits.
org: Southeast University, Max Planck Institute for Informatics, StepFun and others
note: The judge rates visual consistency, visual quality, instruction following and knowledge plausibility. NeurIPS 2025 accepted the paper.

name: KWV Bench
description: Models answer atomic visual questions extracted from tasks distilled from real knowledge-work scenarios.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: L-Eval
description: Models answer over 2,000 queries on 508 long documents of 3k to 200k tokens across 20 subtasks. Scoring uses exact match and judge-model ratings.

name: LAB-Bench
description: Multiple-choice tasks on practical biology research skills: literature, protocols, sequence and figure reasoning, database lookup.
note: 2,457 multiple-choice questions in eight subtasks. 1,967 public on Hugging Face, 489 held back by FutureHouse. Superseded by LABBench2 in 2026.

name: LAB-Bench CloningScenarios
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions about multi-step molecular cloning workflows. CloningScenarios subset of LAB-Bench.
note: 33 public questions on multi-plasmid cloning workflows. PhD researchers score about 60%. LABBench2 carries a 14-task open-response cloning config.

name: LAB-Bench FigQA
description: Models interpret figures from biology papers and answer multiple-choice questions. FigQA subset of LAB-Bench.
note: Anthropic reports LAB-Bench subsets separately in its RSP bio sections.

name: LAB-Bench LitQA2
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions whose answers appear once in recent biology papers. Built to need literature search rather than recall. A LAB-Bench subtask.
note: 199 questions public. PhD researchers score about 70%. FutureHouse PaperQA2 RAG agent matches experts. One of eight LAB-Bench subtasks.

name: LAB-Bench ProtocolQA
description: Models find and fix errors in lab protocols in multiple-choice form. ProtocolQA subset of LAB-Bench.
note: Anthropic reports LAB-Bench subsets separately in its RSP bio sections.

name: LAB-Bench SeqQA
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions that require DNA and protein sequence manipulation. SeqQA subset of LAB-Bench.
note: Anthropic reports LAB-Bench subsets separately in its RSP bio sections.

name: LAB: Contracts
description: 500 in-house contracting tasks (drafting, redlines, issues lists, escalation memos) across 10 contract categories. All-pass expert-rubric grading.
note: Scores reported on a 50-task official hold-out. No public leaderboard as of the Tenet post (2026-08), so every score is Harvey's own run. Each negotiation stage is graded as a separate step, so it does not yet test autonomous end-to-end negotiation.

name: LAB: Diligence
description: Agent researches a synthetic M&A virtual data room (thousands of documents, up to ~80M tokens) and drafts a diligence memo scored against planted-issue rubric criteria.
note: Open-sourced as RL environments (tasks/diligence held 11 data rooms on 2026-10-22). Long-context and exhaustivity stress test. Harvey reports harness design (an RLM root agent over a REPL) moves scores more than model choice. Harvey's RL results use held-out data rooms.

name: LAB: US Case Law
aliases: Legal Agent Bench US Case Law
description: Agents draft a litigation brief for the same party and motion as a real filed federal brief, from the case record. Model judges compare briefs pairwise and wins become Elo ratings.
note: 100 environments built from RECAP dockets and CourtListener opinions. Each runs closed-book with cited cases supplied or open-book with a CourtListener MCP. Opus 5.5 rated highest at launch.

name: LABBench2
description: 11 biology research sub-tasks (literature, figures, tables, patents, trials and more) with tool access. Macro-averaged accuracy.
note: 1,912 tasks in 16 dataset configs. Answers are open-response rather than multiple choice, so scores are not comparable with LAB-Bench. Configs include litqa3, protocolqa2, seqqa2, figqa2, tableqa2, suppqa2, dbqa2, cloning, and the new patentqa, sourcequality and trialqa. Frontier model accuracy falls 26 to 46 points against LAB-Bench. CC-BY-SA-4.0, gated download.

name: LABBench2 FigQA2
description: Models read scientific figures and answer in open response. Served as images or as PDFs. The FigQA2 subtask of LABBench2.
note: 101 tasks in the figqa2 config of the LABBench2 dataset. Open response replaces multiple choice, so scores are not comparable with the LAB-Bench subtask.

name: LABBench2 LitQA3
description: Models answer open-response questions whose answers appear once in recent biology papers. The LitQA3 subtask of LABBench2.
note: 168 tasks in the litqa3 config of the LABBench2 dataset. Open response replaces multiple choice, so scores are not comparable with the LAB-Bench subtask.

name: LABBench2 ProtocolQA2
description: Models find and fix errors planted in published lab protocols, answering in open response. The ProtocolQA2 subtask of LABBench2.
note: 125 tasks in the protocolqa2 config of the LABBench2 dataset. Open response replaces multiple choice, so scores are not comparable with the LAB-Bench subtask.

name: LABBench2 SeqQA2
description: Models reason about DNA and protein sequences and answer in open response. The SeqQA2 subtask of LABBench2.
note: 400 tasks in the seqqa2 config of the LABBench2 dataset. Open response replaces multiple choice, so scores are not comparable with the LAB-Bench subtask.

name: LADDER
aliases: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
description: Policies, orchestrators and frontier-model agents do 145 long-horizon tabletop tasks of 1 to 10 subgoals in three simulators. A task counts only when every object ends in place.
note: Suites are RoboLab-Long (44 tasks), SimplerEnv-Long and RobotArena-Long. Best system 63.3%, falling to 34.8% at 8 to 10 objects. LADDER-Lite is a 10-task subset with GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5.

name: Lakera B3 (Backbone Breaker Benchmark)
description: Crowdsourced prompt-injection attacks hit backbone LLMs inside agent threat snapshots at three defense levels. The score is attack resistance, 100 minus the board's vulnerability percentage.
org: Lakera + ETH Zurich + UK AISI + Oxford
note: A lab result may use another attack subset than the board.

name: LAMBADA
description: Models predict the last word of narrative passages where humans can guess it only from the whole passage. Scored by accuracy.
org: University of Trento and University of Amsterdam

name: Landing Page Arena
description: Models create landing pages. Pairwise votes determine the published Arena rating.
note: The official API publishes an Arena rating, confidence interval and vote count. Voter identity requires confirmation from the board description.

name: Language Confusion Benchmark
description: Models answer prompts in 15 languages and must reply in the language the user wants, both in monolingual and crosslingual settings. A language detector scores line-level and word-level pass rates.
note: The Command A technical report gives crosslingual line-level pass rates on it. EMNLP 2024.

name: Last Secure Code Benchmark
description: Agents rebuild code that a real vulnerability once affected, from a specification that never mentions security. Hidden tests check function and replay an exploit.
org: Alibaba Qwen Team, Alibaba Cloud security and National University of Singapore
note: 450 tasks from 150 vulnerability scenarios, 115 from real CVEs and 35 expert written. Seven languages and 24 CWE classes. Each scenario appears at function, file and repository level. The headline metric counts a task only when both the function and security suites pass. Apache 2.0, also on Harbor Hub and Docker Hub.

name: Last Translation Benchmark
description: Strong models translate hard texts chosen to stay unsaturated, and experts assess the outputs instead of automatic metrics that can be reward-hacked.
note: 40 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: LatchBio Capabilities v1.0
description: LatchBio cross-benchmark suite of agentic biological data analysis (transcriptomics, epigenomics, variants, pharmacology) with deterministic graders.
note: The V1 Capabilities score on benchmarks.bio is a weighted mean of 13 LatchBio benchmarks. They are the SpatialBench, scBench, EpiBench, VariantBench, MetagenomicsBench, TxBench, BioSecBench and OncologyBench sets. Legacy V0 scores are not comparable with V1. Fireworks lists the suite as BioBench.

name: Lazy investigation (Anthropic)
aliases: Avoiding harmful actions from misleading evidence
description: Agents debug a failing job where misleading evidence invites a harmful action such as cordoning a healthy node. Scored 0 to 10 by a grader.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. Every problem expects no action, so it also measures willingness to act.

name: Lazy investigation on misleading codebases (Anthropic)
description: Models trace small, intentionally misleading codebases to answer how a value is set. Score is the share of lazy investigations ending in a wrong answer.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. A different design from the later lazy investigation debugging task scored 0 to 10.

name: LBM Eval
description: Bimanual robot policies run 49 manipulation tasks in the Drake simulator from random starting conditions. Scored by success rate per task.
note: About 125 GitHub stars. Version 1.1.0 (fall 2025) is newer than the snapshot the LBM 1.0 paper used, and the README says it may not reproduce the paper. TRI's VLA Foundry cards score 16 seen and 3 unseen tasks.

name: LBPP (Less Basic Python Problems)
description: Models write Python solutions to 161 new problems built to avoid training-set contamination. Hidden tests score pass@1.
note: The Command A report adds parallel C++, Java, JavaScript, Go and Rust versions.

name: LeanDojo Benchmark
description: Models prove theorems from Lean's mathlib library inside the Lean proof assistant, which checks every proof. The benchmark has 98,734 theorems and proofs with premise annotations. A novel-premises split tests whether a prover can use lemmas it never saw in training.
note: NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track. Versions exist for Lean 3 and Lean 4, and results depend on the mathlib snapshot. It is also a training set. About 850 GitHub stars.

name: Learn2Play Bench
description: Agents play unfamiliar games whose rules are not given and must learn from experience across episodes. Improvement over repeated play is the measure.
note: 55 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: Lech Mazur Creative Writing
description: Models write short stories that must use 10 assigned elements such as characters, objects, and motivations. Judge models compare matched stories pairwise.
note: Earlier versions used 0 to 10 rubric ratings, which the current pairwise ranking replaces.

name: Leetcode (easy)
description: Models solve 41 easy Leetcode problems that OpenAI selected. Scored as problems solved.
note: In-house OpenAI problem set from the GPT-4 Technical Report exam table.

name: Leetcode (hard)
description: Models solve 45 hard Leetcode problems that OpenAI selected. Scored as problems solved.
note: In-house OpenAI problem set from the GPT-4 Technical Report exam table.

name: Leetcode (medium)
description: Models solve 80 medium Leetcode problems that OpenAI selected. Scored as problems solved.
note: In-house OpenAI problem set from the GPT-4 Technical Report exam table.

name: LeetCode Weekly Contest
description: Models solve 126 LeetCode contest problems from July to November 2023. A solution counts only if it passes all of its 20+ test cases.

name: Legacy-Bench
description: Agents debug, add features to and migrate enterprise code in COBOL, Java 7, BASIC, C89, Fortran and Assembly. A task passes only when hidden tests all pass.
note: 100 tasks. Factory added it to the Fireworks index on 2026-09-24, where Fireworks runs it on 12 models.

name: Legal Research Bench
description: Agents answer US federal and state legal research questions with case-law and web tools. Expert rubrics, all-pass and weighted scores by LLM judge.
note: Proprietary questions written by practicing lawyers. Vals runs every model. The board uses all-pass scoring. OpenAI's Astra for Law claim used 200 private validation questions run by OpenAI, not Vals.

name: LegalBench
description: Models do 162 legal reasoning tasks written by legal professionals, covering six types of legal reasoning such as issue spotting and rule application.
note: Vals AI runs it on 151 models.

name: LegalReasonBench
description: Models work long-horizon legal matters built by practicing lawyers, writing memoranda and court filings across dependent assignments, in closed-record and open-research settings.
note: Rule and application scores drop 11 to 38 points when models must find the law themselves.

name: LEGO-Puzzles
description: Vision-language models answer LEGO assembly questions, from basic spatial understanding to planning several assembly steps. The elementary set has 1,100 questions over 11 tasks.
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory and collaborators (Tang, Duan et al.)
note: A second task set asks models to plan step by step. VLMEvalKit supports it.

name: Legora BAR
description: Models work private legal cases end to end inside Legora's agent harness, with the matter's documents and templates. An LLM judge scores outputs against rubrics written by lawyers.
note: Cases span 30 practice areas and seven task families. Results are shown relative to the average of the models run, 17 models in the 2026-10 edition. Legora reruns it as models and harness change.

name: Leipzig Benchmark
description: Models answer 100 research-level math questions with known answers, written by 49 mathematicians at a Max Planck Institute workshop in April and May 2026.
org: Benchmarks in Leipzig workshop at MPI MiS (49 mathematicians), board on ScienceBench (Christian Stump)
note: Two questions stayed unsolved after heavy-thinking runs in mid 2026, and one after the September 2026 re-run with tools. The questions are printed in the paper appendix.

name: LengthCtrl (Qwen)
description: Models do creative writing tasks with length requirements. The score depends on the gap between output length and target length.
note: In-house Qwen evaluation. The data is not public.

name: LengthCtrl (Tencent)
description: Models write text that must meet a requested length, in a Tencent in-house test. Task and scoring details are not published.
note: Seen in the Hunyuan-A13B-Instruct card. Scoring method is a guess from the task type. Qwen reports an in-house test with the same name (lengthctrl-qwen), and we could not tell if they share data.

name: LEXam
description: Models answer 7,537 questions from 340 law exams at Swiss, EU and international law courses, in English and German. Open answers are judged against reference answers, and multiple-choice items are exact match.
note: ICLR 2026. The makers corrected multiple-choice annotation errors in November 2025 and split the choices into 4, 8, 16 and 32 option files.

name: LEXam-hard
description: Agents with legal research tools answer the 518 LEXam open questions that strong open models score lowest on. Questions answerable from memory or unanswerable from their text are removed.
note: A filtered copy of the LEXam open_question test split, joined back to LEXam by id.

name: LexGLUE
description: Models solve a suite of English legal text tasks drawn from court cases, EU law, contracts and terms of service. Most tasks are classification, and one asks for the holding of a US case. Each task reports micro and macro F1.
note: The suite was built for fine-tuned encoder models such as Legal-BERT, and each task ships with training data. About 270 GitHub stars, and the repo was last pushed in 2025-07.

name: LHAW
description: Agents face 285 underspecified variants of long-horizon tasks with goals, constraints, inputs or context removed. Scored on strategic clarification and task success.
note: Variants come from three source benchmarks through a reusable underspecification pipeline. CC BY 4.0.

name: LIBERO
description: Simulated Franka tabletop tasks in four 10-task suites. Policies fine-tuned on 50 demos per task. Success rate over ~50 trials.
note: Saturated: 22 of 35 catalog models self-report >=97% four-suite average. Protocols differ by paper. The same models score 0.02-24.4% on RoboDojo. Papers move to LIBERO-Plus/PRO.

name: LIBERO-MAX
description: Robot policies face 8,000 paired cases where the scene changes during execution, such as a target moving, the viewpoint shifting or an obstacle appearing.
note: Eight change types. Builds on LIBERO. About 340 GitHub stars.

name: LIBERO-Para
description: VLA policies run LIBERO tasks with over 4,000 paraphrased instructions that vary object and action wording separately. Scored by success rate and the difficulty-aware PRIDE metric.
note: EMNLP 2026 main conference oral. 78 Hugging Face paper upvotes. Seven VLA setups lose 22 to 52 points under paraphrasing. A CALVIN-Para variant ships in the same repo.

name: LIBERO-Plus
aliases: In-depth Robustness Analysis for Vision-Language-Action Models
description: LIBERO policies run 10,030 perturbed tasks across seven dimensions: layout, camera, robot start state, language, light, background and sensor noise. Success rate.
org: Fudan University + Tongji University + Shanghai Innovation Institute + NUS
note: Drop-in replacement for the LIBERO package. Camera and robot start-state changes cut most VLAs from about 95% to under 30%. Separate from LIBERO-PRO, by a different team.

name: LIBERO-PRO
description: LIBERO policies tested under object, position, instruction, task and environment perturbations. 50 episodes per task. Success rate.
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology + Harvard + MIT + others
note: Exposes memorization: position and task perturbations drive most models near 0 while object and semantic stay ~0.9. Small, frozen table.

name: LibraryDesignBench
description: An author agent designs a software library from an open spec. Three fresh agents then solve 242 problems with it, and the library scores by their pass rate and code simplicity.
org: SprocketLab (University of Wisconsin-Madison) with Snorkel AI
note: 15 tasks in Rust, Python, TypeScript and Haskell. Each trial scores pass rate squared times simplicity. The board has 11 runs.

name: LibriSpeech
description: Models transcribe English audiobook speech. Scored by word error rate on the test-clean and test-other splits.
note: About 1,000 hours of read speech from LibriVox. Released at ICASSP 2015.

name: LifeSci Diamond
description: Models write regulatory affairs deliverables for drugs, biologics and medical devices, such as change assessment memos, dossier inconsistency logs and agency letters. The 55 tasks span five families: reporting categories, Module 2/3 dossier consistency, missing evidence, submissions and correspondence, and device vigilance. A model judge grades each answer against a task rubric, and a task passes only when every rubric line is met and no penalty fires.
note: Arca sells regulatory AI software and ranks four configurations of its own product next to 18 plain model APIs. Ten tasks are public (CC BY 4.0) and 45 are held out. The 2026-11-04 edition regraded every answer with one judge, GPT-6.1 Sol at medium effort, so earlier numbers are not comparable. Each system gave one answer per task, and one task moves the pass rate by 1.8 points. Of the 55 answer keys, 26 had specialist review, 18 were written by contributors without a second read and 11 rest on primary sources only. The repository had 1 GitHub star on 2026-11-05.

name: LifeSciBench
description: Models complete 750 expert-written life science research tasks, often with attached figures, tables, or sequence files. Graded against expert rubrics as score and pass rate.
note: 750 expert-authored tasks over seven workflows and seven biological domains. 1,062 task artifacts, 173 scientist contributors, 19,020 rubric criteria and 453 expert reviewers. Launched 17 June 2026.

name: LifeVal
description: Assistants carry out everyday personal tasks rather than advise on them: finding childcare, booking a car inspection, ordering groceries on a budget, handling government paperwork. Tasks come from time-use surveys and from about 100 people who recorded tasks they wanted an assistant to handle. Score is average reward across tasks.
note: OpenAI reports only its own models, and there is no public leaderboard. OpenAI says it used LifeVal internally for a year before the launch.

name: LingoQA
description: Models answer free-form questions about short driving videos. A trained classifier, Lingo-Judge, scores whether each answer is truthful.

name: LinguaSafe
description: Models face 45k safety prompts in 12 languages, from Hungarian to Malay. Direct and indirect assessments score harmful responses, and an oversensitivity test checks over-refusal.
note: Data mixes translated, transcreated and natively sourced prompts. The Apertus report gives severity-weighted scores by harm category and language.

name: Linguini
description: Models solve 160 International Linguistic Olympiad problems with 894 questions in 75 mostly low-resource languages. All evidence needed is in the context.
org: Meta, University College London and University of the Basque Country
note: Reports give whole-problem exact match or per-question accuracy, so check the metric.

name: LinuxArena
description: AI-control setting in live Linux production-like environments. Measures stealthy side-task completion against action and CoT monitors.
note: 20 environments, 1,667 main tasks and 185 side tasks. The public repo holds 10 environments, 919 main tasks and 93 side tasks with trajectories for 11 models. LaStraj adds human-made attack trajectories.

name: LisanBench
description: Models build the longest chain of distinct English words from a given start word, each differing from the last by one letter. The score sums valid chain lengths over all start words.
note: Three trials per start word, averaged. A difficulty-weighted score gives common words less weight. The site also tracks reasoning tokens and full-run cost. Tokenization affects letter-level tasks like this one.

name: LiveBench
description: Models answer monthly refreshed questions across math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis. Scored automatically against objective ground truth.

refreshes.label: New coding questions and a spatial reasoning task
New questions for all three math tasks
Refreshed instruction following, Connections and Zebra puzzles
Newer coding, typos and plot questions, and 2024 AMC problems
New coding questions on real libraries, refreshed data analysis
Refreshed tasks against saturation and contamination
Added a logic and navigation task
Added a math task and a data analysis task

changes.text: The maintainers removed the house-traversal task after fixing ambiguous answer parsing revealed saturation. Scores thereafter cover a different set of tasks.

The maintainers reran agentic coding with Mini-SWE-Agent and raised the step limit from 50 to 250. They replaced the existing leaderboard results, so earlier scores use a different scaffold and budget.

note: A rolling benchmark that refreshes questions by dated release, and scores are tied to a release. The newest questions are withheld from the public set. Releases since 2025 added agentic coding (2025-05-30), refreshed tasks (2025-11-25) and added tasks on 2025-12-23 and 2026-01-08.

name: LiveClawBench
description: Agents act as OpenClaw personal assistants on 134 multi-step tasks across 10 app domains backed by stateful mock services. A run passes when its reward exceeds 0.8.
org: Mosi-AI (Xiang Long, Yehui Tang and collaborators)
note: The paper evaluates 17 agents from eight model families, three runs per case, using the Harbor framework. Tasks include 12 safety cases and are labeled Easy, Medium or Hard.

name: LiveCodeBench
description: Competitive programming problems collected after model cutoffs from LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces. Scored pass@1 on hidden tests.

changes.text: The LiveCodeBench maintainers added tests to the lite code-generation dataset. Earlier evaluations used a different test collection, which can change whether a generated program passes.

note: Rolling time windows (v5, v6) make cross-card comparison hard. Top models near 90%.

name: LiveCodeBench Pro
description: Continuously updated Codeforces, ICPC and IOI problems annotated by olympiad medalists. Reported as Elo.
note: Problems come in quarterly and half-year splits, from 2024 Q4 to 2025 Q3 with 144 to 207 problems each. Labs report different splits, so scores often do not compare. The livecodebenchpro.com site now returns 404.

name: LiveCodeBench v5
description: Competitive programming problems collected after model cutoffs from LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces. Scored pass@1 on hidden tests.
note: Problems released from May 2023 to January 2025, 880 in all.

name: LiveCodeBench v6
description: Competitive programming problems collected after model cutoffs from LeetCode, AtCoder, Codeforces. Scored pass@1 on hidden tests.
note: Problems released from May 2023 to April 2025, 1,055 in all.

name: LiveMACE
description: Agents trade in live financial markets, and the benchmark scores the process capabilities behind their decisions, not only returns.
note: 57 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: LiveMath
description: Models solve 250 math problems written with six professional mathematicians. The sets are 150 regular high school problems, 50 at about AIME level and 50 multimodal problems with figures.
note: Some problems appeared as HiddenMath in the Gemini 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5 Pro reports, and the rest are new. Google calls it a living benchmark with versioned releases.

name: LiveMathBench
description: Models solve recent competition math problems, sampled many times. The G-Pass@k metric rewards both peak accuracy and stable answers across samples.
note: Releases are dated, such as v202412 and v202505, so scores from different releases are not comparable. Not Google DeepMind's LiveMath. The paper has 92 HF upvotes.

name: LiveMathematicianBench
description: Models answer multiple choice questions about theorems from arXiv papers published after their training cutoff. Wrong options follow plausible but invalid proof sketches.
org: Linyang He, Nima Mesgarani and others
note: The question set is refreshed from new arXiv papers, so scores depend on the snapshot. ByteDance Seed reports it in the Seed2.1 model card.

name: LiveResearchBench
description: Deep research agents write cited reports for user-centric questions that need current information from many live web sources. Rubric-based judges score the reports.
note: 121 GitHub stars. Deep research model reports cite it next to BrowseComp and GAIA.

name: LiveSecBench
description: Models answer Chinese-language prompts that probe safety across areas such as legality, ethics, factuality and privacy. The paper's first edition turned a judge's pairwise comparisons into Elo ratings. The leaderboard's March 2026 edition gives each model an overall score from 0 to 100. The question bank is updated in dated editions.
org: Intoken (隐拓智安) and academic coauthors
note: The questions are not published, only the harness and results. The paper's first edition (v251030) scored 18 models. The leaderboard now shows a March 2026 edition. 29 GitHub stars and 4 HF paper upvotes, so traction rests on the maintained leaderboard.

name: LiveSports-3K
description: Video models give real-time commentary and answer questions on sports clips. An LLM judge scores the free-form commentary.
org: Chen et al. (LiveCC team, NUS Show Lab and ByteDance)
note: Introduced with the LiveCC model at CVPR 2025. The ByteDance affiliation is inferred from the author list.

name: LiveSQLBench
description: Contamination-resistant text-to-SQL on PostgreSQL with hierarchical knowledge bases, including CRUD tasks. Scored by soft execution match and test cases.
note: Gold SQL and test cases are withheld from the public dataset and sent by email request. Base-Full v1 (600 tasks) came out in 2025-09. LiveSQLBench-Large-v1 (March 2026) adds 480 tasks on databases with about 54 tables each. Version 1.5 is announced.

name: Llama 2-Chat helpfulness human evaluation (Meta)
description: Three human raters compare Llama 2-Chat with a rival chat model on about 4,000 single and multi-turn helpfulness prompts.
note: In-house Meta evaluation. Results are win, tie and loss rates against one rival per model size.

name: Llama 2-Chat safety human evaluation (Meta)
description: Human raters score responses to about 2,000 adversarial prompts on a five-point scale. Ratings of 1 or 2 count as violations.
note: In-house Meta evaluation. The paper shows violation percentage and mean rating only in charts.

name: Llama 3 pairwise human evaluation (Meta)
description: Human raters compare Llama responses with a rival model on about 7,000 prompts across six capabilities and three multiturn sets.
note: In-house Meta evaluation. Results are win and loss rates per capability and rival, with no overall score.

name: Llama internal safety benchmarks (Meta)
description: Models face Meta's adversarial and borderline prompts per capability and language. Scored as violation rate and false refusal rate.
note: In-house Meta evaluation with over 4,000 prompts per capability or language. Llama 3 shows results only in charts.

name: Llama verbatim memorization probe (Meta)
description: Models get prompts sampled from their pretraining data. The score is the share of generations that reproduce the true continuation verbatim.
note: In-house Meta measurement on pretrained models, reported for several prompt and continuation lengths.

name: LLaVA-Bench (In-the-Wild)
description: Multimodal assistants answer open questions about a small set of diverse real images. A GPT-4 judge scores each answer relative to a reference answer.
note: Introduced with the LLaVA paper. Scores are a relative ratio, so the judge model version matters.

name: LLM Chess
description: Models play chess in multi-turn dialogs against a random player or the Komodo Dragon engine. The board reports wins, Elo and game duration, which tracks instruction following.
note: Dragon was added as a stronger opponent for Elo anchoring once reasoning models beat the random player. Paper at NeurIPS 2025 FoRLM workshop. About 140 GitHub stars.

name: LLM Colosseum
description: Two models each control a fighter in Street Fighter III and choose moves from text descriptions of the game. Wins give Elo ratings.
note: Made at a Mistral hackathon. The repo has about 1,484 stars and was last updated on 2025-03-21.

name: LLM Confabulation Leaderboard
description: Models answer misleading questions about recent articles whose answers are not in the text. The board ranks confabulation rate against non-response rate.
note: 201 human-checked questions as of 2025-02-10. About 250 GitHub stars.

name: LLM training task (Anthropic)
description: Agents optimize a CPU-only small language model training implementation. Scored by speedup.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: LLM-AggreFact
description: Models judge whether claims are supported by a grounding document across 11 pooled datasets, such as RAGTruth and ExpertQA. Scored by balanced accuracy.
org: UT Austin + Salesforce AI Research (Tang, Laban and Durrett)
note: Introduced with the MiniCheck fact checker (EMNLP 2024). The leaderboard lists 47 models, mostly fact-checking models with some general LLMs.

name: LLM-WikiRace
description: Models play the Wikipedia game: starting from one article, they follow one hyperlink at a time to reach a target article. At each step the model sees only the links on the current page, and a game is lost after 30 steps. Three difficulty levels are set by the shortest path between the two pages. Scores are the share of games won at each level.
org: University of Oxford, University College London and University of Basel
note: The leaderboard lists 30 models and also reports tokens per step. It gives no update date, and its newest entries are from early 2026. The paper finds that world knowledge helps only up to a point, after which planning limits success. About 10 HF paper upvotes and 8 GitHub stars.

name: LLMBoxing
description: People see one question with two anonymous model answers and pick the better one. The site counts preferences between model pairs.
note: Independent human preference site cited in the Mistral 7B paper. The domain now serves an unrelated gambling page, so only archived copies of the leaderboard remain.

name: LMArena (Elo)
description: People chat with two anonymous models side by side and vote for the better reply. Votes become Elo-style ratings for each model.
note: The 2025 paper The Leaderboard Illusion reported that some labs tested many private variants before release. Arena changes vote filters and the rating fit over time, for example two bias terms added on 2026-05-12, so old and new ratings drift. Arena Expert, added 2025-11-05, ranks the hardest 5.5% of prompts.

name: LMArena Image Edit Arena
description: Image editing models apply the same user edit request to the same image, anonymously and side by side. Community votes give Elo-style ratings.
note: Ratings are published in the image_edit config of the dataset.

name: LMArena Image-to-Video Arena
description: Video generation models animate the same input image with the same prompt, anonymously and side by side. Votes give Elo-style ratings.
note: Shares votes infrastructure with the Text-to-Video Arena. Launched on the web on 2026-01-21.

name: LMArena Search Arena
description: People compare answers from two anonymous search-augmented models on their own questions and vote for the better one. Votes become Bradley-Terry ratings.
note: Collection began on 2025-03-18 and the announcement post is dated 2025-04-15. Ratings move as votes arrive, so a score belongs to its snapshot date. Since about 2026-07 the default rating blends in labeled factuality battles at a 25% weight.

name: LMArena Text-to-Image Arena
description: Image generation models answer the same user prompt side by side and anonymously. Community votes between the two images give Elo-style ratings.
note: LMArena announced the arena in December 2024 and opened the leaderboard in January 2025, per posts found in search. Ratings are in the text_to_image config of the dataset.

name: LMArena Text-to-Video Arena
description: Video generation models make clips from the same text prompt, anonymously and side by side. Votes from logged-in users give Elo-style ratings.
note: Video Arena moved to the web on 2026-01-21 with 15 video models. It ran earlier in another venue, per the blog.

name: LMArena Video Edit Arena
description: Video editing models apply the same edit request to the same clip, anonymously and side by side. Community votes give Elo-style ratings.
note: Launch month not found. Ratings are in the video_edit config of the dataset.

name: LMBuild
description: Language model agents design 3D structures as parts, joints, materials and assembly steps. Scoring checks that the structures can be built and work as intended.
note: It had 38 Hugging Face paper upvotes and 7 GitHub stars.

name: LMCA
aliases: A dataset of rated conceptual arguments
description: Models rate arguments against position texts on philosophy, decision theory, and AI risk. Scored by agreement with expert ratings, with a ceiling near 85.
org: Emery Cooper, Caspar Oesterheld, and collaborators
note: Same benchmark as the lmca record, from the same arXiv paper 2607.27499.

name: lmgame-Bench
description: Models play platformer, puzzle and narrative games such as Sokoban, Tetris, 2048 and Candy Crush through a Gym-style API with perception and memory scaffolds.
note: Labs report per-game scores. UI-TARS-2 reports six games with no aggregate.
