description: Models get unsafe requests across a fine-grained taxonomy of topics and linguistic variations. A judge model scores whether each answer refuses or complies.
note: Dataset versions are dated, such as 202406 and 202503. The Hugging Face dataset is gated.

name: SoSBench
description: Models answer hazardous requests drawn from real regulations in six scientific fields. Scored by how often the model complies with a request it should refuse.
note: 3,000 prompts over chemistry, biology, medicine, pharmacology, physics and psychology. Prompts were grown from real laws by a model-assisted pipeline that adds misuse scenarios.

name: SpaCE-10
description: Models answer more than 5,000 questions about indoor 3D scenes that test 10 atomic and 8 compositional spatial abilities.

name: SpaceXAI internal R&D evals
description: Internal xAI model-development tasks (MTS Eval) and production inference-stack patches (InferenceEval).

name: SpaceXAI MTS Eval
description: Agents do model-development tasks from xAI engineers, such as diagnosing reward hacking and debugging training infrastructure, under fixed budgets.
note: In-house xAI evaluation with 29 tasks in the standard non-GPU suite.

name: SPAR-Bench
description: Spatial perception and reasoning questions over single and multiple views of indoor 3D scenes, from depth and distance estimates to object relations and spatial imagination.
org: Zhang et al. (From Flatland to Space)

name: SpatialBench (LatchBio)
description: Agentic spatial-transcriptomics data analysis problems with deterministic graders. Anthropic reports a 115-problem Verified variant.
note: Three problem sets carry this name. The December 2025 paper has 146 problems, the June 2026 repo is a revised set of 159, and Anthropic cards report SpatialBench Verified with 115. Scores on different sets do not compare.

name: SpatialBench (Ropedia)
aliases: SpatialBench: Is Your Spatial Foundation Model an All-Round Player?
description: Spatial foundation models are tested across many 3D tasks, viewpoints, scene domains, input densities and hardware limits, beyond the domains they were trained for.
note: NeurIPS 2026. 69 HF paper upvotes. Not the LatchBio SpatialBench for biology.

name: SpatialBench-Long
description: Agents run long, multi-step analyses of real spatial biology datasets that need sustained biological reasoning.
note: Part of LatchBio's BioBench suite on benchmarks.bio. The V1 set has 21 evaluations. Release month is the GitHub repo creation month.

name: SpatialEval Maze-Nav
description: Models answer questions about routes and turns in mazes given as text or images. 1,500 multiple-choice questions scored by accuracy.
note: Phi reasoning reports use the text-only 10 by 10 version.

name: SpatialEval Spatial-Map
description: Models answer questions about relations and counts among objects placed on a map given as text or images. 1,500 questions scored by accuracy.
note: Phi reasoning reports use the text-only version.

name: SpatialSense VQA
description: Models judge whether a stated spatial relation between two objects holds in an image. The relations were crowdsourced to defeat simple cues.
org: Princeton Vision and Learning Lab (Kaiyu Yang, Olga Russakovsky, Jia Deng)
note: Gemma 3 reports a VQA-style version for pretrained checkpoints, not the original classification setup.

name: SpatialTree
description: Organizes spatial abilities into a hierarchy, from low-level perception to mental mapping, simulation and agentic use, and tests vision-language models at each level.

name: SpatialViz-Bench
description: Models answer 1,180 generated multiple choice puzzles on mental rotation, mental folding, visual penetration, and mental animation. Scoring is accuracy.
note: A program generates the questions, which limits training contamination. Humans score about 82%.

name: SpatialWorld
description: Multimodal agents act in real-world style environments to show interactive spatial understanding, rather than answer static spatial questions.
note: 50 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: SpatialWorld Digital
description: Agents complete entertainment tasks in digital environments. The score is the published digital task success rate.
note: One track of SpatialWorld. The SpatialWorld record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: SpatialWorld Physical
description: Agents complete tasks in physical environments. The score is the published overall success rate across physical task categories.
note: One track of SpatialWorld. The SpatialWorld record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: SPBench
description: Spatial perception and reasoning questions built from ScanNet scenes. A single-image set covers distance, size and direction, and a multi-view set adds counting across views. Answers are numbers or multiple choice.
note: Reports do not always say whether a score is the single-image set, the multi-view set or both.

name: Speaker identification
description: Speech models get audio requests to identify a speaker by voice. Scored on refusing when they should and complying for famous quotes.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Cards report should refuse and should comply rows with no overall number.

name: Speech Agent Arena
description: People hold live conversations with two hidden speech-to-speech agents on the same scenario, some with tool calls, then pick the one they preferred. Votes are fit to an Elo rating, and the arena also tracks task success.
note: Ratings move as votes arrive, so a lab post freezes a value that later drifts.

name: Speech Arena
description: Models generate speech. Listeners compare outputs, and pairwise votes determine Elo ratings.
note: The Bradley-Terry view estimates the same vote pool and remains an auxiliary metric.

name: Speech-to-Speech Index
description: Artificial Analysis's combined score for speech-to-speech models.
note: xAI quotes the index in its Grok Voice 3 launch post.

name: SpeechRole
description: Speech role-playing agents talk in character across 98 roles. A model judge scores interaction ability, speech expressiveness and role fidelity from the generated speech.
note: Released with a 111k-conversation training set (SpeechRole-Data). Qwen reports scores above 100, so the scale is not a percentage.

name: SPEED-Bench
description: Measures speculative decoding across varied prompts and domains. Reports the average acceptance length of draft tokens, so higher means faster generation at the same output.
note: Scores depend on the draft method and draft length, so labs report the split and settings next to each number.

name: SpeedrunBench
description: Agents try to finish goals in 10 video games as fast as possible. Score is time to goal in frames or seconds, lower is better.
note: Agent writes an input tape and scoring runs in a separate container. Public repo covers the three open-source games. HF dataset is gated.

name: SPI (security patch identification)
description: Models decide whether code commits from open-source projects are security patches.
note: Dataset from SPI: Automated Identification of Security Patches via Commits, ACM TOSEM 2021. Google reports accuracy.

name: Spider
description: Models turn natural language questions into SQL over 200 multi-table databases from 138 domains. Test databases are unseen in training, and answers are scored by exact match or execution.
org: Yale University (LILY lab, Tao Yu et al.)
note: 10,181 questions and 5,693 unique SQL queries annotated by 11 Yale students. The Spider site announced Spider 2.0 as its successor in 2024.

name: Spider 2.0
description: Models and agents write SQL for real enterprise databases with large schemas, across BigQuery, Snowflake, SQLite and dbt projects. Answers are checked by executing them.
org: XLANG Lab, The University of Hong Kong, with collaborators
note: Three settings: Spider 2.0-Snow, Spider 2.0-Lite and Spider 2.0-DBT, which replaced the original agent setting in 2025-05. The maker updates examples over time, so scores can drift.

name: Spider2-V
description: Multimodal agents do data science and engineering workflows in real enterprise apps such as BigQuery, dbt and Airbyte, on a desktop computer. Execution-based checks score each task.
note: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks. Built on OSWorld infrastructure. Different from the text-to-SQL Spider 2.0.

name: Spiral-Bench v1.0
description: Models chat for 20 turns with a simulated suggestible user played by Kimi-K2. A judge logs protective and risky behaviors such as pushback, sycophancy and delusion reinforcement, which combine into a safety score.
note: Added to eqbench.com on 2025-08-15. Covered by The Decoder and Hacker News, and later papers reuse its 20-turn setup. Now a legacy board.

name: Spiral-Bench v1.2
description: Models chat for 20 turns with a simulated suggestible user. A judge ensemble of Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 and Kimi-K2 logs protective and risky behaviors with intensity ratings, which combine into a safety score.
note: Version 1.2 went live on 2025-10-12 with a judge ensemble, a reworked rubric and new behaviors. It drops findings of intensity 1, so scores differ from v1.0.

name: SpireClimb
description: Agents play Slay the Spire 1 and 2 at max difficulty through a computer-use harness on fixed seeds. Score is the mean win rate.
note: Top human players win ~85% (StS1) and ~95% (StS2). Seeds are not published.

name: SpireClimb StS1 A20 Heart
description: Agents play Slay the Spire 1 through its graphical interface at Ascension 20 and must defeat the Heart. Scored by win rate over fixed seeds.
note: Epoch expects saturation within a few model generations because labs may train on the game.

name: SpireClimb StS2 A10
description: Agents play Slay the Spire 2 at Ascension 10 through screenshots and mouse and keyboard, 15 runs per character. Scoring is the win rate.
note: Epoch AI froze the game at v0.107.1, and top human players win about 95 percent of runs.

name: SplatBench
description: A model rebuilds an object in 3D from eight photos by placing up to 300 Gaussians itself through tool calls, with no optimizer. Half of the 30 tasks start from an empty scene, and half ask it to reassemble a scrambled fit. SplatScore compares renders from eight angles the model never sees, with an empty scene at 0 and gradient descent at 100.
note: Scores can be negative, because misplaced Gaussians cover background that an empty scene gets right. Each model ran every task twice at medium effort. A single Gaussian in the object's average color scores 4.2, and every model stays below gradient descent with 64 Gaussians, which scores 67.7. Two scanned scenes are for non-commercial research only. There is no human baseline yet.

name: SpotSoundBench
description: Models find the time span of short sound events hidden in long, unstructured YouTube recordings. It has 400 audio, query and timestamp triplets.
note: Released with the SpotSound method paper. Qwen reports it as audio grounding.

name: SpreadsheetBench
description: Real spreadsheet manipulation questions from Excel forums. Output workbook is checked cell-by-cell against reference solutions.
note: Kimi K3 reports 'SpreadsheetBench 2'. We did not find a separate public repo for v2.

name: SpreadsheetBench 2
description: Agents complete 321 expert-annotated business spreadsheet workflows, such as financial modeling, debugging, and charting, in multi-sheet workbooks. Scoring is task accuracy.

name: SpreadsheetBench Verified
description: Models solve 400 real spreadsheet manipulation questions from Excel forums, an expert annotated subset of SpreadsheetBench. Each answer runs against several test spreadsheets.
org: Renmin University of China (RUCKBReasoning) with Shortcut.AI
note: Scores are not comparable with the full 912 question set. The maker leaderboard has a separate V1 Verified (400) tab.

name: SQuAD
description: Models extract answer spans from Wikipedia paragraphs for over 100,000 crowdsourced questions. Scored by exact match and F1.
note: Saturated, with models above human performance since 2018. SQuAD 2.0 added unanswerable questions.

name: SQuAD v2
description: Models extract answers from Wikipedia paragraphs and must abstain on over 50,000 adversarial unanswerable questions. Scored by exact match and F1.
note: Saturated. The test set is hidden, so cards report the dev set.

name: SQuALITY
description: Models write question-focused summaries of public-domain short stories. Outputs are scored against human-written reference summaries with ROUGE.

name: SRE-Bench
description: Software reverse engineering without source: 262 binary instances from 19 private programs, each with six graded objectives.
note: Programs are private to stay contamination-free.

name: SSH stress-testing evaluation (Anthropic)
description: Models continue prefilled conversations about suicide and self-harm built from anonymized user feedback. Score is the rate of appropriate course correction.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: StableToolBench
description: Models solve user requests by calling tools from ToolBench's large set of real-world APIs. A virtual API server with a cache and API simulators stands in for live APIs, so results stay stable over time. GPT-4 judges whether each request was solved and which of two answers is better, giving a solvable pass rate and a win rate.
note: It evolves from ToolBench, which the almanac carries, and changes the scoring, so its scores are not comparable with ToolBench's. The judge model and the simulated API answers both shape the scores. About 240 GitHub stars.

name: STALE
description: Agents with long-term memory must notice when a later observation quietly makes an earlier memory false. The benchmark has 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios and 1,200 queries over more than 100 everyday topics, with contexts up to 150K tokens. Queries test whether the model spots the outdated belief, rejects a false premise and acts on the new state.
note: 47 Hugging Face upvotes. No code or data link was listed on the paper page on 2026-11-05. Tests both frontier LLMs and dedicated memory frameworks.

name: Standard jailbreaks (xAI)
description: Models face a battery of published and internal jailbreaks. Compliance is the share of should-refuse attacks that get disallowed help.
note: In-house xAI evaluation. The Grok 4.5 card calls it Jailbreaks.

name: Standard Refusal Evaluation
description: Models answer disallowed and benign safety-related prompts across policy categories. An autograder scores not_unsafe and not_overrefuse.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Some cards give category scores only.

name: STARE
description: Models solve 4K spatial tasks such as 2D and 3D transformations, cube net folding, tangrams, perspective and temporal reasoning that people solve by visual simulation.
org: University of Washington, Sun Yat-sen University and Stanford University
note: Models score near chance on cube net folding and tangram tasks in the paper.

name: STaRK
description: Retrieval systems find the right items for complex queries over knowledge bases that mix free text with relations between entities. The three domains are product search, academic paper search and precision medicine. Most queries are synthesized and checked by people, and a smaller set is written by people.
note: Entries are retrieval systems, many built on language-model embeddings or rerankers, not chat models. Results report ranking metrics such as Hit@1 and MRR. About 340 GitHub stars.

name: StarSkirmish Bench
description: Each model gets one hour in its lab's own CLI to write a StarCraft: Brood War bot in C++. The score is its win rate against human-written bots.
note: v0.2 (2026-10-15) replaced v0.1 with new flagship models and first-party harnesses. Each model has five runs.

name: STATE-Bench
description: Agents work multi-step enterprise tasks in travel, customer support and shopping with a sandbox database, domain tools and a simulated user. They must apply the right policy.
note: 450 tasks. A second Agent Learning Track adds train trajectories and a retrieval hook for memories or skills. Reports pass@1, pass^5 and a UX rating.

name: STATE-Bench Main 0.7.0
description: Agents complete enterprise tasks in travel, customer support, and shopping. The score is overall pass@1 for this track and version.
note: The first dated submission is 2026-05.

name: StateBench
description: Models follow variables through long runs of assignments and report a final value. Four tiers share one source trace and differ only in the update: fixed values, reassignment, self-referential updates, and assignment by reference. Problems come in several formats, such as code, spreadsheet edits and people moving between rooms, at lengths from under 2K to over 2M tokens.
note: Not Microsoft's STATE-Bench, an enterprise agent benchmark. The tiers follow Krohn–Rhodes theory. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna, and Gemini 3.8 Flash fall to 13% or lower on the longest problems of the hardest tier. Open pretrained models stay at chance on that tier.

name: Static Jailbreak Evaluations
description: Models face a fixed set of jailbreak attacks on bio, violence and cyber requests. Scored as defender success rate per category.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Cards report category scores with no overall number.

name: Stealth and Situational Awareness evaluations
description: Prerequisite-scheming challenges: stealth tasks (circumventing oversight) and situational-awareness tasks (reasoning about own deployment).
note: Open-source in Inspect Evals (gdm_stealth, gdm_self_reasoning). External review found many SA tasks test one ability.

name: STEM Professor Bench
description: Agents solve unpublished research problems written by professional scientists. Most problems concern theoretical physics, with some partial credit.
note: Anthropic reports 64 problems and nine attempts per problem. A model grades 56 problems, while author procedures grade eight.

name: Step Race
description: Several models talk in public, then secretly pick moves in a race where colliding moves cancel. The game tests cooperation and deception.
note: The repo was created on 2025-01-21 and updated on 2025-12-09.

name: Step-SWE-Bench
description: Models fix software issues inside several coding agent harnesses, such as Claude Code, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. The score is the average over harnesses.
note: StepFun calls it in-house. The post gives per-harness scores for six harnesses and does not describe the tasks.

name: StepCodeBench
description: Models do software engineering tasks in 553 repositories, across 9 task types, 20 application domains and 33 languages. Task types include feature changes, bug repair, refactoring and environment setup.
note: StepFun built it in house and reports avg@4. The post does not say how answers are graded. The same table lists StepCode-Bench-Daily and StepCode-Bench-General rows with different scores.

name: StereoSet
description: Models choose between stereotypical, anti-stereotypical and unrelated completions in four domains: gender, profession, race and religion. Scores combine language modeling and stereotype preference.
org: MIT, Intel AI and McGill University
note: The ideal stereotype score is 50.

name: Stick to Your Role!
description: Models simulate populations of fictional personas and answer personal-values questionnaires in many different conversation contexts. The benchmark measures how stable the expressed values stay across contexts, both for each persona and for the ranking of personas within the population.
note: The leaderboard lists 32 open-weight models, the newest from 2025, and its Space has 63 likes. It reports several stability metrics, not one headline number.

name: StockBench
description: Agents trade stocks over a fixed evaluation window. StockBench ranks models by the mean of final return, maximum drawdown and Sortino ratio. The score is the board's rank, so a lower score is better.
note: Built to be contamination-free by using recent market windows. 58 HF paper upvotes and about 180 GitHub stars.

name: Story Cloze Winter 2018
description: Systems select the correct story ending on the Winter 2018 test set. CodaLab reports percentage accuracy under submission identities.
note: Systems select the correct story ending on the Winter 2018 test set. CodaLab reports percentage accuracy under submission identities.

name: StoryCloze
description: Models pick the correct ending for a four-sentence everyday story from two candidate endings. Scored by accuracy.

name: StrataBench Land v1
description: Models classify land instruments, extract lease terms, and distinguish petroleum terms in three separate benchmarks. Classify and Extract have their own records. Define publishes three measures without one headline score.
note: Collide explicitly forbids averaging its three tasks into one score. Models receive separate Extract results for natural and schema prompts. Collide licenses data under CC BY-NC 4.0 with additional permission to run benchmarks and publish attributed scores.

name: StrataBench Land v1 Classify
description: Models identify the legal act performed by each of 66 synthetic land instruments. Collide scores label accuracy under open and closed prompt protocols.
note: One benchmark of StrataBench Land v1. The suite publishes no combined score. Collide has not published Classify baseline scores. Collide reports 11 sampled parent types while grading against 23 allowed labels.

name: StrataBench Land v1 Extract
description: Models extract ten shared lease fields from 628 synthetic instruments. Collide divides correct field decisions by correct, omitted, and wrong decisions, excluding unscored fields.
note: One benchmark of StrataBench Land v1. The suite publishes no combined score. Collide reports natural and schema prompts on the same ten fields. Collide keeps the schema protocol’s additional four fields outside the headline score.

name: StrategyQA
description: Models answer 2,780 yes or no questions that need implicit multi-step reasoning, such as whether Aristotle used a laptop. Scoring is accuracy.
org: Mor Geva et al. (Tel Aviv University and Allen Institute for AI)

name: StreamBench (StreamChat)
description: Video models answer questions on streaming videos across media types, including multi-turn interaction and reasoning tasks.
note: Published at ICLR 2025 with the StreamChat framework. It is a different test from StreamBench for language agents (arXiv 2406.08747).

name: StreamEval
description: Streaming video generation models handle 300 scripted cases of 15 to 300 seconds. Requests arrive over time across avatar dialogue, performance, world generation and editing.
note: 85 HF paper upvotes and about 610 GitHub stars two weeks after release.

name: StreamingBench
description: Models answer questions while a video streams in, as a human viewer would. It tests real-time visual understanding, omni-source understanding and context understanding.
note: Qwen reports it as audio-visual interaction.

name: StrongREJECT
description: Forbidden-prompt jailbreak benchmark with a rubric grader that scores how useful a non-refusal actually is.
note: HF copy linked by Mistral is a third-party mirror (walledai).

name: StrongREJECT v2 (Meta)
description: Models face a cascade of jailbreak attacks on disallowed behaviors adapted from StrongREJECT plus internal ones. Reports attack success rate.
note: Meta variant of public StrongREJECT with internally curated behaviors and a multi-turn LLM attacker.

name: StructEval
description: Models generate or convert structured outputs in 18 formats, such as JSON, TOML and HTML. StructEval-T covers text-only formats and StructEval-V renderable ones.
note: 2,035 examples over 44 task types. Published in TMLR in January 2026.

name: Structural Biology (Anthropic)
description: Models answer questions about a biomolecule's function from structural data and basic tools, in multiple-choice and open-ended variants.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. Cards report the two variants separately with no overall score.

name: Structured expert probing campaign: chem-bio novel design
description: Biosecurity and chemistry experts test whether a model helps design novel chem-bio threats. Scenarios are rated against Preparedness risk levels.
note: Results are counts of scenarios per risk level, not a score.

name: Structured expert probing campaign: radiological and nuclear
description: Radiological and nuclear experts test whether a model helps with weapons development steps. Conversations are rated against Preparedness risk levels.
note: Results are counts of conversations per risk level, not a score.

name: Structured Output Benchmark
description: Models turn a text context into JSON that must match a given schema and hold the right values. The 5,324 records come from multi-hop questions, OCR text of documents and meeting transcripts, all given to the model as text. Seven automatic metrics, such as value accuracy, faithfulness and JSON validity, combine into an overall score that weights hard schemas more.
note: Interfaze sells extraction models and ranks two of its own models on its leaderboard of 30. Runs use temperature 0 with reasoning off, and a few models could only run at their lowest reasoning setting. The text records come from HotpotQA, the image records from olmOCR-bench and the audio records from AMI meetings. About 30 GitHub stars.

name: Structured Translation (Cohere)
description: Models translate JSON and similar structures, either whole or only named fields. Metrics check parsing, schema match, untranslated or wrongly copied fields and line counts.
note: In-house Cohere evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: StudentBench
description: AI tutors teach real students GRE material and are scored by the students measured learning gains. A second study has expert tutors compare AI lesson plans and practice problems.
note: 13 AI tutors and expert human tutors taught 2,383 participants. Handshake reports AI tutoring as statistically equivalent to expert human tutoring on GRE gains.

name: StudyArena Audio
description: Models produce audio responses to user prompts. Anonymous human comparisons determine the published rating in this separate vote pool.
note: Only entries with observed ballots count as results. Topic filters do not form separate benchmark records.

name: StudyArena Image
description: Models produce image responses to user prompts. Anonymous human comparisons determine the published rating in this separate vote pool.
note: Only entries with observed ballots count as results. Topic filters do not form separate benchmark records.

name: StudyArena Text
description: Models produce text responses to user prompts. Anonymous human comparisons determine the published rating in this separate vote pool.
note: Only entries with observed ballots count as results. Topic filters do not form separate benchmark records.

name: Subversion Strategy Eval
description: Models must devise and execute strategies to subvert control protocols without shared memory between calls.
note: Anthropic cards report a subset of the environments.

name: Success detection (Google DeepMind)
description: Embodied reasoning models judge from robot camera images or video whether a manipulation task succeeded. Later versions use raw video to catch mid-execution failures.
note: Google reports image-based and video-based splits, and earlier single-view and multi-view splits for Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6. Release month is the Gemini Robotics 1.5 era and is likely, not verified.

name: sudo L7
description: Coding agents get staff-level engineering requests in mostly private production codebases. Graders score whether the agent found hidden risks and shipped the right change.
note: 60 tasks. Each model runs in its own developer's coding agent.

name: Sudoku-Bench
description: Models solve Sudoku variants with unusual rule sets that need creative, multi-step deduction. Scored by the share of puzzles solved.

name: Suicide & Self-Harm evaluation
description: Static and dynamic chats with suicidal or self-harm signals test adherence to prevention practice and crisis resources. Reports policy adherence rate.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Suicide and self-harm evaluations (Anthropic)
description: Models handle single-turn and multi-turn conversations about suicide and self-harm. Score is the appropriate response rate.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Suicide Memory Bench
description: AI systems, each a model in its own app or coding harness, talk with 128 fictional personas over 29 chats. Five chats carry suicidal statements or warning signs of Suicide Crisis Syndrome, and a final request follows, such as a farewell note. Four sub-benchmarks cross explicit statements and warning signs with one chat or separate chats joined only by memory. A model judge rates each reply on a 0 to 4 safety scale.
note: Version 01.1, with 2,048 cases for each system. Built with 22 licensed clinicians. Scores run from 0 to 4. Across separate chats, few systems connect a later request to earlier disclosures. The data is licensed, not public.

name: Summary of a Haystack
description: Models read a synthetic haystack of conversation or news documents where specific insights repeat, then write a query-focused summary that cites its sources. An automatic evaluation scores insight coverage and citation accuracy.
note: The paper tested 10 long-context LLMs and 50 RAG systems. Humans score about 56% on the joint score, and long-context models without retrieval scored under 20%. The paper has 87 HF upvotes.

name: SummScreenFD
description: Models write a recap of a TV episode from its full transcript. Plot details sit in dialogue scattered across the episode, so the model must find and join them. Scores compare outputs with human-written recaps using ROUGE.
org: Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago and collaborators
note: SummScreen has two parts, and FD is the ForeverDreaming part that SCROLLS uses. The almanac carries SCROLLS as a suite. Microsoft reports it in the Phi-3.5 long-context table. About 40 GitHub stars.

name: SUNRGBD
description: Models detect objects in about 10,000 indoor RGB-D images and predict their 3D bounding boxes. Scored by average precision.

name: SUPERB
description: Self-supervised speech models are tested as frozen encoders on a range of speech tasks, including speech recognition, keyword spotting, speaker identification, intent classification and emotion recognition. Each task trains only a light prediction head on top of the shared model.
note: SUPERB scores speech encoders such as wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT and WavLM, not end-to-end voice assistants. The 2,568 GitHub stars belong to the S3PRL toolkit that runs it. Each task keeps its own metric, so sources often report a few tasks, not one number.

name: SUPERChem
description: Models solve 500 expert-written chemistry reasoning problems, offered in multimodal and text-only forms. Expert solution paths also allow a reasoning path score.
note: Humans scored 40.3% at release and GPT-5 (High) scored 38.5%. ByteDance Seed reports the text-only form.

name: SuperCLUE
aliases: SuperCLUE 中文通用大模型测评基准
description: The CLUE team tests Chinese and foreign language models on periodic sets of Chinese questions covering language, professional knowledge, reasoning, agents and safety. Open answers are graded by a strong LLM judge, and results feed an overall ranking.
note: Each period uses new questions, with reports such as 2023-12, 2024 H1, 2025 H1, 2025-09 and the 2025 annual report. Scores from different periods are not comparable. The repository has over 3,300 stars.

name: SuperCLUE-Agent
description: Chinese language models are tested on agent skills in Chinese tasks. These include tool use with several API calls, task planning and memory over long dialogues.
note: The board is updated from time to time with more Chinese models. The repository has about 96 stars.

name: SuperCLUE-Math6
description: Models solve thousands of multi-step Chinese math word problems. Scores combine reasoning-step quality and accuracy into a comprehensive score and a reasoning level.
note: Reports give a comprehensive score, a reasoning-steps score, an overall accuracy score and a reasoning level from 1 to 5.

name: SuperCLUE-RAG
description: Chinese models answer questions twice, first without documents and then with supplied documents. A judge model compares the answers to rate how well the system uses retrieved text.
note: The repository has about 133 stars. It also includes questions with no documents.

name: SuperCLUE-Safety
description: Chinese language models answer 4,912 open-ended safety questions over more than 20 sub-dimensions in multi-round adversarial dialogues. Follow-up turns push harder than the first prompt.
note: Built after China's generative AI rules took effect on 2023-08-15. The paper tested 13 models. The board last added models on 2024-01-04.

name: SuperGLUE
description: Models solve eight English language understanding tasks, including BoolQ, COPA, MultiRC, ReCoRD, RTE, WiC, and WSC. Scored by the average task score.
org: NYU, Facebook AI, University of Washington, and DeepMind
note: Saturated, with models above the human baseline since 2021.

name: SuperGPQA
description: 26,529 graduate-level multiple-choice questions across 285 disciplines. Accuracy.

name: SuperMatBench
description: Models answer materials chemistry questions in a QA part and solve materials tasks with tools in an Agent part.
note: Known only from a one-line footnote in the Ling-3.1-flash model card. No paper, dataset or repository was found, so the scoring method is a guess.

name: SURDS
description: Models answer spatial questions about objects in nuScenes driving camera images across six single-object and multi-object tasks. Scoring is task accuracy.
org: Xianda Guo et al. (Wuhan University and partners)
note: The first arXiv version was called DriveMLLM before the authors renamed it SURDS.

name: Surface Evolver Bench
description: Agents write Surface Evolver datafiles that model liquid surfaces under physical constraints across 16 tasks. Deterministic checks give partial credit for matching hidden reference quantities.
note: Only one example task is public, and the scored tasks and grading scripts stay hidden.

name: Surge AI blind coding evaluation
aliases: Surge AI blind human coding eval
description: Surge AI raters blindly score model coding outputs on a 1-5 scale. Mistral reports five models.
note: Lab-commissioned human eval (Mistral with Surge AI). Tasks and rubric not public.

name: SusVibes
description: Coding agents rebuild a feature in a real open-source Python project from a plain-language request. Each task comes from a historical vulnerability fix, so the original human version was insecure. Hidden functional tests and security tests check the result. Scores report the share of solutions that work and the share that are also secure.
note: Endor Labs runs it as the Agent Security League, a public board of agent harness and model pairs (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, SWE-agent). Endor added an anti-cheating check because some agents read the git history to recover the original fix. The paper and Endor describe 200 tasks across 77 CWE types, while the repository README now lists 186. The repository has about 57 GitHub stars and names ICML 2026 as the venue.

name: SVAMP
aliases: Simple Variations on Arithmetic Math word Problems
description: Models solve 1,000 grade-school arithmetic word problems. The problems are variations of problems from earlier datasets, made to catch solvers that ignore the question or the word order. The final numeric answer is scored by exact match.
note: NAACL 2021. Google's chain-of-thought paper (Wei et al. 2022) used it with GSM8K and MAWPS. Saturated for current models. About 142 GitHub stars.

name: SVG-Bench (MiniMax)
description: Model creates or edits SVG graphics from text or image prompts. A VLM checks results, averaged over 3 runs.
note: Lab-created in-house eval (MiniMax).

name: Swarm Bench
description: Models orchestrate agent swarms on complex tasks that benefit from coordinated decomposition and parallel execution.
note: In-house Moonshot AI evaluation. The K2.5 report lists WildSearch, Batch Download, WideRead and Long-Form Writing domains. Tasks are not public.

name: SWE agentic fabrication eval
description: A grounding autorater checks whether claims made by coding agents on long SWE tasks are supported by tool outputs.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: SWE Atlas
description: Scale's coding-agent suite beyond patching: codebase Q&A, writing production tests, and refactoring in real repos. Rubric/test-scored leaderboards.
note: This record covers SWE Atlas Codebase QnA (124 tasks), whose dataset and leaderboard it links. Test Writing and Refactoring have their own records.

name: SWE Atlas Codebase QnA Extended
aliases: Mercor SWE Atlas Codebase QnA Extended
description: Agents answer questions about large codebases, graded with rubrics. Mercor adds 50 new expert-written tasks to the 124 public ones and reports both scores.
note: Held-out extension of swe-atlas. Mercor shows the original and extended score for each model. The month is approximate. The Wayback Machine first saved the earliest extended pages on 2026-08-15.

name: SWE Atlas Refactoring
description: Coding agents refactor code in 70 tasks in real repositories with internet access cut off. Tests and software-quality rubrics grade the result.
note: One of three SWE Atlas leaderboards, added last in May 2026.

name: SWE Atlas Test Writing
description: Coding agents write production-quality tests for 90 tasks in real repositories with internet access cut off. Programmatic checks and rubrics grade the tests.
note: One of three SWE Atlas leaderboards. Labs report it apart from Codebase QnA, for example as SWE Atlas-Test Writing.

name: SWE Atlas v1.1
description: Scale's coding-agent suite beyond patching: codebase Q&A, writing production tests, and refactoring in real repos. Rubric/test-scored leaderboards.
note: Combined index over QnA, Test Writing, and Refactoring. Separate category boards remain distinct.

name: SWE Refactor Bench
description: Agents migrate 20 whole open-source repositories to a new language, framework, platform, or build system. Graded by migration audit, behavioral tests, and adversarial verifier models.

name: SWE-bench
description: Models resolve 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories. A patch counts as resolved when the hidden repository tests pass.
note: The original set behind SWE-bench Lite (March 2024) and SWE-bench Verified (August 2024).

name: SWE-bench CLI
description: Agents make verified multi-file changes in unfamiliar open-source repositories across 200 tasks, 11 languages and 10 technical domains. Harbor runs fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass test suites on the result.
note: Not part of the Princeton SWE-bench family. The board reports Pass@1.

name: SWE-bench Lite
description: Models resolve 300 self-contained GitHub issues chosen from SWE-bench to cut evaluation cost. Hidden repository tests decide each patch.
note: Widely used by agent papers in 2024 before SWE-bench Verified took over.

name: SWE-bench Multilingual
description: 300 GitHub-issue tasks across nine programming languages in SWE-bench format. Patch graded by repository tests.
note: Released with SWE-smith. Paper link is the SWE-smith paper.

name: SWE-bench Multimodal
description: SWE-bench tasks whose issues include screenshots or design mockups from visual JavaScript repos. Patch graded by hidden tests.

name: SWE-Bench Pro
description: 1,865 long-horizon issue-resolution tasks from 41 repos in four languages. Agent patch must pass hidden tests. Pass@1.

changes.text: The maintainers published results without the previous cap limit. Comparisons with earlier capped runs must account for the different execution budget.
The maintainers removed outdated unit tests, including tests requiring the year 2025, and tests included by mistake. Earlier and later verifiers can judge the same patch differently.

note: 731 public, 858 held-out and 276 commercial tasks. Copyleft repos reduce contamination. Vendor-reported scores differ from Scale runs. In 2026-06 Cursor found that 63% of successful Opus 4.8 Max solves looked up the fix. With git history sealed and no internet, that score fell from 87.1% to 73.0%.

name: SWE-Bench Pro Private
description: Agents resolve held-out software issues from the private SWE-Bench Pro split. The leaderboard reports the percentage of resolved tasks.

name: SWE-Bench Pro V2
description: Agents resolve 642 repaired issue tasks from the SWE-Bench Pro public split in Go, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript. A locked protocol re-grades each patch in a clean container.
note: Audits and expert review repaired or retired 480 of the 731 v1 public tasks and dropped 89. The agent can reach only the model endpoint. V2 scores are not comparable with v1. The dataset default config is V2 since 2026-09-22.

name: SWE-Bench Pro V2 Hard
description: Agents resolve the 51 SWE-Bench Pro V2 tasks that at least two of five model families failed. Graded with the V2 locked protocol.
note: The paper reports Hard scores from 52.9 to 98.0 while the full V2 set reaches 99.4. It is the hard config of the V2 dataset, and three of 54 candidates were removed after expert review.

name: SWE-Bench ProMax
description: Agents do 170 expert-curated, large refactoring tasks from real commits in Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++ and Rust, with rewritten issue descriptions.
note: 81 HF paper upvotes. Not made by Scale AI and not a version of SWE-Bench Pro.

name: SWE-bench Science
description: Coding agents fix 119 repository-level tasks from 98 scientific software projects in 20 domains, split into issue-driven, expert-exploratory and integration tasks. Tests check each fix.
org: Fudan University OpenMOSS (Zhipeng Xu et al.)
note: The best agent, Claude Code with Opus 5 at max effort, stayed below 50 percent pass@1. Not part of the SWE-bench family. 64 HF paper upvotes.

name: SWE-bench Verified
description: 500 human-validated GitHub issues from 12 Python repos. Agent writes a patch that must pass hidden tests.

changes.text: The maintainers fixed grading for 662 truncated test identifiers in Verified. Passing tests that previously counted as missing can now receive credit.
The maintainers added test exit-code checks to detect forged passing output. Patches that spoof test results can no longer receive the same credit.

note: Near-saturated. Absent from 2026 Anthropic/OpenAI headline tables. OpenAI cards use it only inside CoT-Control.

name: SWE-bench Verified (hard subset)
description: Agents solve a subset of SWE-bench Verified tasks estimated to take a human engineer more than one hour.
note: Anthropic RSP autonomy evaluation built on public SWE-bench Verified tasks.

name: SWE-bench Verified Extended
description: Agents resolve real GitHub issues by editing codebases, scored by repository tests. Mercor adds 50 new expert-written tasks to the 500 public ones and reports both scores.
note: Held-out extension of swe-bench-verified. Mercor shows the original and extended score for each model. The month is approximate. The Wayback Machine first saved the earliest extended pages on 2026-08-15.

name: SWE-bench Verified hard subset (Meta)
description: Agents fix the hardest SWE-bench Verified issues. Meta uses about 42 tasks and a 50% indicative threshold for AI R&D risk.
note: Meta's own hard subset. It may differ from Anthropic's SWE-bench Verified hard subset.

name: SWE-bench-Live
description: Agents resolve recent GitHub issues gathered by an automated pipeline, with 50 new verified Python tasks added each month. Tests in a docker sandbox check each patch.
note: MultiLang (January 2026, 1,077 tasks in 8 languages by August 2026) and Windows (March 2026) splits have their own leaderboards. Scores depend on the snapshot month.

name: SWE-bench-Live Verified
description: Task success on the official Verified split. The source reports each submission denominator separately. Other language and platform splits remain separate.
note: Task success on the official Verified split. The source reports each submission denominator separately. Other language and platform splits remain separate.

name: SWE-CI
description: Agents maintain a repository from a base commit toward a later reference commit over 100 commit pairs, looping through tests, requirement writing and code changes.
note: An architect agent turns test gaps into requirements and a programmer agent implements them. Scores track whether correctness holds across the change sequence. 183 GitHub stars.

name: SWE-Clar
description: Agents question a simulated client about an incomplete request, then build greenfield software from real Upwork jobs. Acceptance tests score the build.
note: 100 tasks from jobs that each paid at least US$4,000. A separate run scores the agent's answers about client requirements. 9 models at release.

name: SWE-Dev
description: Models implement new features in real Python repositories from requirement documents, across 500 test tasks. Developer-written unit tests decide pass or fail.

name: SWE-EVO
description: Coding agents implement release-note changes in seven mature Python projects, editing about 21 files per task. Large test suites check each of the 48 tasks.
note: The paper reports GPT-5.4 with OpenHands at 25%. The arXiv record reached version 6.

name: SWE-Explore
description: Coding agents are scored on separate repository skills, such as understanding, context retrieval, code localization and bug diagnosis, instead of one pass or fail.
note: 122 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: SWE-fficiency
description: 498 tasks in nine Python data/ML/HPC repos: agent must speed up a real workload without breaking tests. Scored as speedup relative to expert patch.
note: Replay study (arXiv 2607.01211) found 411/498 tasks keep a valid signal and a few low-speedup tasks dominate the score weight.

name: SWE-Interact
description: Coding agents work 75 multi-turn software tasks driven by a simulated developer who adds requests over a long session.
note: Ships as Harbor run configs. Paper submitted 2026-06-29.

name: SWE-Lancer
description: Models complete real Upwork software tasks, from bug fixes to features, and pick between engineering proposals. Scored by end-to-end tests and payout earned.
note: Only the Diamond split is public. Some cards report dollars earned rather than pass rate. Since 2025-07-17 the public repo holds 198 of the 237 IC SWE Diamond tasks. OpenAI dropped 39 tasks that failed offline, so later scores use a smaller set.

name: SWE-Lancer Diamond (SWE Manager)
description: Models review competing implementation proposals for real freelance tasks and pick the best one. Scored against the original choice as pass@1.
note: Manager split of SWE-Lancer. The swe-lancer record covers the IC SWE split.

name: SWE-Marathon
description: 20 realistic multi-hour software tasks (library reproductions, product clones, ML work). Verifiers combine hidden tests, parity and integrity checks.
note: No configuration exceeds 30% pass@1. Reward hacking seen in 13.8% of rollouts. Labs ran H20-recalibrated branches. v1.0 scores (k=5) sit on an archive board pinned to v1.0-official, and v1.1 replaced it in July 2026.

name: SWE-Marathon v1.1
description: Agents complete 20 multi-hour software tasks such as library rebuilds, product clones and ML work. Hidden tests, parity checks and integrity checks grade each run, scored over 8 trials.
note: The maker keeps v1.0 scores on an archive board. v1.1 moved the post-training task to H100 GPUs and raised trials from 5 to 8.

name: SWE-Perf
description: Agents speed up code in 140 tasks drawn from performance pull requests in real GitHub repos. Scored on correctness and runtime gain.

name: SWE-PI
description: A coding agent does a bug-fix task in a repository seeded with an injected payload that tries to exfiltrate a secret. Reports attack success rate.
note: In-house Meta benchmark. 142 scenarios from 50 SWE-bench instances.

name: SWE-PolyBench
description: Coding agents resolve 2,110 tasks from 21 repositories in Java, JavaScript, TypeScript and Python. Tasks cover bug fixes, features and refactors, checked by execution.
note: A stratified 500-task subset (SWE-PolyBench500) is common.

name: SWE-rebench
description: Agents fix fresh GitHub issues that an automated pipeline mines each month. Tests decide whether the issue is resolved.
note: Scores depend on the monthly task window, so results from different months are not directly comparable.

name: SWE-Review
description: Models review code changes in several languages and scenarios to find defects. Scores reflect defect recall and the rate of hallucinated defects.
note: In-house: MiniMax never released the tasks or the formula that combines recall and hallucination rate.

name: SWE-sweep
description: Agents get a real repository with no hint of bug type or location and must find and repair as many bugs as they can. Score is the share of bugs resolved.
org: Meta Superintelligence Labs (with Harvard, UW and Stanford)
note: 100 repositories with 4.1k bugs, run through Harbor with mini-SWE-agent. Authors include the SWE-bench team.

name: SWE-Together
description: Coding agents work through 109 repository tasks rebuilt from real multi-turn sessions between users and coding agents. A simulated user replays the original user's goals and gives feedback when the agent needs it. Scores count tasks solved and the number of corrections the user had to make.
note: Tasks come from 11,260 recorded sessions. The makers' leaderboard runs 23 models in one harness (opencode) with two trials each. Five entries are paper results that were not rerun. A judge score of 0.85 or more counts as a solve. About 86 GitHub stars.

name: SWebBench
description: Agents browse the web to retrieve information and do research tasks. iFlytek built it in house.
note: The Spark-X2.6-4B card says it will be open-sourced soon. Grading is not described.

name: SwitzerlandQA
description: Models answer four-option questions on Swiss geography, history, social life, politics and insurance at national, cantonal and commune level. Items come in five languages.
org: Swiss AI Initiative (EPFL, ETH Zurich, CSCS)
note: Swiss AI built it for the Apertus report, with 9,167 items per language across 26 cantons. The listed Hugging Face dataset was not reachable on 2026-11-01.

name: SWM-Bench (Social World Models)
aliases: Building Social World Models with Large Language Models
description: Predict how Kalshi and Polymarket belief trajectories shift after news events. 12k+ points across politics, finance and crypto, chronologically split.
note: Chronological train / Polymarket-test / Kalshi-test split limits leakage. Baselines are time-series foundation models. ICML 2026.

name: SWT-bench
description: Agents write tests that reproduce real GitHub issues from SWE-bench repositories. Scored by the share of tests that fail before and pass after the fix.
note: Reported on Lite and Verified splits, so check which one a card uses.

name: Sycophancy evaluation (offline)
description: Models answer a fixed set of messages resembling production traffic that could elicit sycophancy. A grader assigns a sycophancy score.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. Scores run from 0 to 1, lower is better.

name: Sycophancy on user-provided prompts (Anthropic)
aliases: Non-sycophantic response rate on re-sampled challenging conversations
description: Models continue real feedback conversations where earlier Claude models were sycophantic. Score is the non-sycophantic response rate.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation built from user feedback conversations. The prompts are not public.

name: Sycophancy prompts (Anthropic)
description: Models answer single-turn prompts that invite sycophancy, such as bad business ideas or delusional beliefs. Four synthetic sets and one hand-written set report sycophancy rates.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The hand-written set targets users with severe mental illness or delusional thinking.

name: SycophancyEval (answer sycophancy)
description: Models answer factual questions where the user suggests a wrong answer. Score is the relative accuracy drop against neutral prompts.
note: xAI used it in the Grok 4 and Grok 4.1 cards. Later xAI cards use an internal sycophancy eval instead.

name: SycophancyEval (Sharma et al.)
description: Models answer questions and give feedback while users state opinions. Measures accuracy shifts and feedback positivity caused by user views.
note: Anthropic system cards replicate the answer bias and feedback bias settings from the paper.

name: SynthDocBench
description: Vision-language models answer questions about synthetic long documents where length, layout, modality and difficulty are varied one at a time to locate failure causes.
note: 68 upvotes on Hugging Face papers.

name: SysBench
description: Models follow 500 system messages across five user turns each. A model verifier checks constraints, instructions and whole sessions.
note: Labs usually report ISR, the instruction-level satisfaction rate.

name: T-Eval
description: Models use tools step by step, and each sub-process is scored separately: instruction following, planning, reasoning, retrieval, understanding, and review.

name: TableBench
description: Models answer 886 questions about real-world tables across 18 fields in four groups: fact checking, numerical reasoning, data analysis and visualization. Fact and numeric answers are scored by exact match, analysis answers by ROUGE-L, and chart code by pass@1.
note: AAAI 2025. In April 2025 the authors released a cleaned test set and new metrics, so earlier scores are not comparable. 53 HF paper upvotes and about 97 GitHub stars.

name: Tacit Knowledge and Troubleshooting
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions on tacit lab knowledge and troubleshooting that need hands-on expertise. Scored as cons@32.
note: OpenAI Preparedness evaluation. The questions are not public.

name: Tacit Knowledge Brainstorm (Open-Ended)
description: Models answer 50 open-ended troubleshooting questions drawn from virologists' and molecular biologists' careers. Scored as pass@1 against an ideal answer.
note: OpenAI treats this evaluation as contextual.

name: TACoS
description: Models find the time span in a cooking video that matches a sentence. Labs score temporal grounding by mean IoU with the annotated span.
org: Max Planck Institute for Informatics (Rohrbach et al.)
note: The corpus came from a GCPR 2014 paper on multi-sentence video description. Later work reused it for temporal grounding. The month is the GCPR conference month.

name: TallyQA
description: Models answer open-ended counting questions about images, including complex ones that need object relationships or attributes. Scored by exact count accuracy.

name: Task-dependent output homogenization evaluation
description: Models answer prompts several times. A judge scores functional diversity where it is wanted and consistency where one answer is right.
note: Reports a homogenization score and a heterogeneity score on a 0 to 1 scale.

name: TASTE
description: 92 pairwise comparisons of AI safety research proposals. Model must match experienced researchers' preference. Accuracy versus ~77% human agreement.
note: Dataset is available on request only.

name: TasteVal
description: 8 AI R&D tasks. Models iteratively design experiments. Taste measured as the compute needed to reach expert-level scores.
note: Tasks kept private.

name: TAT-DQA
description: Models answer questions about financial report pages that mix tables and text, often needing arithmetic. Scored by exact match and F1.
org: NExT++ Research Centre, National University of Singapore

name: TAT-QA
description: Models answer 16,552 questions about 2,757 passages from real financial reports that mix a table with text. Many answers need arithmetic, counting or comparison. Scored by exact match and F1.
org: National University of Singapore (NExT++) and collaborators
note: ACL 2021. The test set answers were released in January 2024, so the hidden test is gone. A document version, TAT-DQA, followed in 2023. About 142 GitHub stars.

name: tau-bench
description: Agents chat with a simulated user and call retail or airline APIs under policy rules. A task passes if the final database matches the goal.

changes.text: The Sierra maintainers corrected retail reference actions and clarified ambiguous user instructions. Earlier revisions can require different actions or mislead the simulated user, affecting task success.
The Sierra maintainers clarified retail test instructions to reduce simulated-user errors. Evaluations before and after this change present different guidance to the user simulator.

The Sierra maintainers required both the final database state and requested outputs to be correct for full reward. The earlier grader could accept correct-looking text despite an incorrect database state.

note: The repo marks its tasks as outdated and points to tau2-bench, now tau3-bench, which fixes airline and retail tasks.

name: tau-bench Airline
description: Agents help simulated airline customers through tools while following airline policies on the original tasks. The score is pass^1 as a percentage.
note: One track of tau-bench. The tau-bench record keeps lab scores that combine tracks. Authors mark these original tasks as outdated and point to later benchmarks with revised tasks.

name: tau-bench Retail
description: Agents help simulated retail customers through tools while following store policies on the original tasks. The score is pass^1 as a percentage.
note: One track of tau-bench. The tau-bench record keeps lab scores that combine tracks. Authors mark these original tasks as outdated and point to later benchmarks with revised tasks.

name: tau2-bench
description: Dual-control customer-service simulations (retail, airline, telecom) where agent and simulated user both act. Graded on final state.
note: τ³-bench (v1.0.0, 2026-03) lives in the tau2-bench repo and adds banking_knowledge and voice modes. V1.0.1 fixed banking grading. Telecom scores depend on the user-simulator model.

name: tau2-bench Verified
description: Agent serves simulated customers in airline, retail and telecom under policies, with Amazon-fixed faulty tasks from τ²-bench. Pass rate.
note: Lab-created verified variant (Amazon AGI) of Sierra's τ²-bench. Fixes documented in FIXES.md.

name: tau2-Noise (LongCat)
description: Agents run tau2-bench tasks after a pipeline injects instruction noise and tool failures into the environment. The score is the average over several noisy copies.
note: In-house robustness variant of tau2-bench. Meituan says it will release the noise injection pipeline.

name: tau3-bench
description: Agents use tools and follow policies while talking with simulated users in airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. Scoring is task success rate.
note: Release 1.0.1 in July 2026 fixed banking grading, so earlier banking scores do not compare, and τ-bench 2.0 followed in October 2026.

name: Tax Agent Bench
description: Agents research 391 expert-written US corporate tax questions with tools and submit one cited written answer. A judge grades it against a rubric and checks that citations are real.
note: Splits are 5 public, 193 licensable validation and 193 private test questions. Main metric is all-pass accuracy, with weighted pass as partial credit. 80 models on the board on 2026-10-29.

name: TaxCalcBench
description: Models compute complete US federal tax returns line by line from taxpayer data, with no tax engine. A return counts only when every evaluated line is exact.
note: Tax Year 2024 edition. The leaderboard still offers a TY 2024 view next to v2.

name: TaxCalcBench v2
description: Models read W-2, 1099 and other PDFs and compute full federal and state returns line by line. A return counts only when every evaluated line is exact.
note: v2 adds realistic PDF inputs, state returns and more complex cases, so scores differ from v1. 50 returns. Fireworks lists 14 models.

name: TaxEval v2
description: Models answer expert-written tax questions. A judge grades answer correctness and stepwise reasoning against expert solutions.
note: Over 1,500 questions: 20 public on request, 300 licensable validation and 1,223 private test. Vals archived it as saturated by 2026-09-01. Release month not stated on the page.

name: TCS-Bench
description: Models write proofs of target results from STOC, FOCS and SODA papers, given the needed context. A verification agent, checked against expert judgments, grades each proof.
org: Google Research + collaborators (Cohen-Addad, Woodruff and others)
note: The reference verifier exceeds 90% accuracy on an expert-labeled set. AINews reported a math system at 71.0%. The repo had 0 stars on 2026-11-01.

name: TEACh
description: Agents complete household tasks in simulated homes, such as making coffee or preparing breakfast, guided by a dialogue between a Commander who knows the task and a Follower who acts. The dataset holds over 3,000 human dialogues and defines three benchmarks: acting from dialogue history, predicting the trajectory from a dialogue, and completing the task as two agents. Scores are task success rates.
note: It runs in the AI2-THOR simulator. About 150 GitHub stars, and the repo was last pushed in 2024-05.

name: TempCompass
description: Video models answer questions about temporal aspects of short clips, such as action order, speed, direction and attribute change, in several question formats.
org: Peking University and Huawei Noah Ark Lab (Liu et al.)
note: Clips come in pairs that differ only in one temporal aspect, so single frames cannot answer them.

name: Template Following generalization (Qwen)
description: Models follow system prompts and emit exactly formatted XML or JSON tool calls for five scaffolds derived from popular IDE and CLI coding agents.
note: In-house Qwen evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Temporal reasoning with search
description: Models with search answer real queries that test date arithmetic, stale facts and time-sensitive context. Reports error rate.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: TemporalBench
description: Video models answer about 10K questions on fine-grained temporal dynamics, built from about 2K detailed human annotations of video clips.
note: The format field is a guess from the question-answer design.

name: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench
description: Coding agents do tasks in four work domains: code, web, office and security. Each task is rebuilt from a real commit or business scenario as a short request that resists web search.
note: Tasks, images, harness, tests and reference solutions are open. The report includes a cross-model leaderboard.

name: Terminal-Bench
description: Agents complete about 80 hard tasks in sandboxed Linux terminals, such as compiling code or configuring servers. Test scripts check the final container state.
note: Terminal-Bench 2.0 replaced this first release in November 2025 with 89 harder tasks, and later versions followed.

name: Terminal-Bench 2.0
description: 89 hard terminal tasks across 16 categories in containers. Hidden tests verify the final state. 5 trials per task.
note: Leaderboard entries are audited and trajectories are public. Later versions exist (Vals now uses Terminal-Bench 4.0).

name: Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified (Z.ai)
description: Agents do the Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks after Z.ai fixed environments for 89 tasks and instructions for 11. A further 2026-08-18 round fixed tests and instructions in 6 more tasks.
note: GLM-5, Step 3.5 Flash and DeepSeek V4 cards report it next to plain Terminal-Bench 2.0, with different scores. Z.ai says its review fed the official Terminal-Bench 2.1.

name: Terminal-Bench 2.1
description: 89 hard terminal tasks across 16 categories in containers. Hidden tests verify the final state. 5 trials per task.

changes.text: The maintainers changed the reward-hacking judge to assess task intent instead of gold-file heuristics. The revised rules can change which successful trials the leaderboard disqualifies.
The maintainers required ATIF trajectories for rewarded trials during submission checks. Submissions without those trajectories now fail intake despite reporting successful tasks.

note: Fixed 28 of the 89 tasks in 2.0. Scores moved by up to 12 points, so the two are kept apart.

name: Terminal-Bench 2.1 Extended
description: Agents complete long command-line tasks in containers, scored by verification tests. Mercor adds 99 new expert-written tasks to the 89 public ones and reports both scores.
note: Held-out extension of terminal-bench-2-1. Mercor shows the original and extended score for each model. The month is approximate. The Wayback Machine first saved the earliest extended pages on 2026-08-15.

name: Terminal-Bench 3.0
description: Agents complete 74 tasks across 7 domains in sandboxed terminal environments. Verifier scripts grade each trial as pass or fail.
note: Released first as FrontierBench v0.1, the name Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 card uses. Terminal-Bench 4.0 succeeded it in August 2026.

name: Terminal-Bench 4.0
description: Agents complete 66 hard tasks in containerized terminals across software, ML, science, security, and operations. Test scripts verify each result, scored as resolution rate.
org: Stanford University, Harbor, and Laude Institute
note: It removed 8 saturated or flawed tasks from Terminal-Bench 3.0 and set a flat 8-hour agent timeout.

name: Terminal-Bench 4.1
description: The Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks with hardened verifiers: agents complete 66 hard tasks in containerized terminals across software, ML, science, security, and operations. Test scripts verify each result, scored as resolution rate.
org: Stanford University, Harbor, and Laude Institute
note: It kept the 4.0 tasks and hardened the verifiers of 44 of them against reward hacking, then regraded the saved 4.0 runs. 162 trials changed score, and every model stayed within its earlier 95% interval.

name: Terminal-Bench Challenges
description: Agents build a large project end to end with no time limit, such as a faster Rust compiler or a WebGL renderer in WebAssembly. Each challenge has its own test bed and metric.
org: Terminal-Bench team (Stanford, Harbor and Laude Institute)
note: Three challenges at launch: Rust compiler speedup, inference engine codegolf and WASM WebGL renderer. Submissions must share the artifact and full agent logs.

name: Terminal-Bench Hard
description: Agents complete 44 hard tasks from Terminal-Bench Core in the Terminus 2 harness. Artificial Analysis scores pass@1 averaged over 3 repeats.
note: Artificial Analysis retired it in June 2026 in favor of Terminal-Bench 2.1.

name: Terminal-Bench-Science
description: 70 scientific research-workflow tasks across five science areas, run in Harbor containers. Hidden tests give the resolution rate.
note: 70 tasks kept from 920 proposals. v0.1. V0.2 in progress. Citation is a Zenodo DOI, no paper.

name: Terminal-X
description: A suite of three terminal datasets for coding agents. DeepTerminalBench tests single-shot depth, EvoCode-Bench tests multi-round iteration and RoadmapBench tests version upgrades on real repositories.
note: The blog post is dated 2026-05-02. All tasks use the Terminal-Bench 2.0 task format and the Harbor framework. The suite has no combined score, so each member is its own record.

name: TERMS-Bench
description: Agents negotiate the price of a single item with simulated counterparts over up to 10 rounds of alternating offers. Counterparts follow six behavior families across three regimes. A program scores each agent from its logged actions on four separate axes: surplus captured, agreement calibration, belief error about the opponent and procedural violations. Extra modes score merchant profit and a bankroll over many sessions.
note: There is no model judge and no composite score, so models are compared axis by axis. The leaderboard data was generated on 2026-05-04 and covers about a dozen models. No code repository is linked.

name: TestPrism
description: Coding agents write tests for 300 tasks. A test passes only if it fails on the starting code, accepts every valid implementation and rejects every invalid one.
note: It had 36 Hugging Face paper upvotes.

name: Text Classification (ByteDance Seed in-house)
description: Models analyze business text and return labels or structured outputs, for example sentiment or the main viewpoints in user content.
note: In-house ByteDance Seed evaluation. The tasks are not public. It seems to follow the Seed1.8 Information Processing set. Scoring is a guess.

name: Text persuasion study on political opinions
description: Participants read model-written articles or chat with a model on political topics. Scored on opinion shift against human-written articles.
note: Human participant study used for the GPT-4o Preparedness persuasion score.

name: Text to Text Safety
aliases: Text to Text Safety (lower is better)
description: An automated content safety evaluation measures policy violations in model answers to text prompts.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. Model cards report only the change in percentage points against an earlier Gemini model.

name: Text-based reinforcement learning task (Anthropic)
description: Agents build scaffolding that improves a weaker model on a text-based reinforcement learning task.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: TextArena
description: Collection of competitive text games for LLM eval and RL, with an online Elo leaderboard.

name: TextCaps
description: Models retrieve matching text and images using the TextCaps corpus.

name: TextEdit
description: Image generation models edit text inside 2,148 real and synthetic images across 18 subcategories. OCR, image-fidelity metrics and a multimodal LLM judge score target accuracy, text preservation and scene integrity.
note: Released with the InternVL-U technical report on 2026-03-06. Each image has a hand-annotated edited ground truth. A 500-sample mini set is also reported.

name: TextEdit Real
description: Models edit text in real images in the full TextEdit test set. The score is the published judged average.
note: One track of TextEdit. The TextEdit record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: TextEdit Virtual
description: Models edit text in virtual images in the full TextEdit test set. The score is the published judged average.
note: One track of TextEdit. The TextEdit record keeps lab scores that combine tracks.

name: TextQuests
description: Agents play 25 classic interactive fiction games. The score is harmful actions per 100 steps, where lower is better. The board also reports game progress.
note: Meta reports the harm rate per 100 steps as a safety measure.

name: TextVQA
description: Models answer 45,336 questions about 28,408 images that require reading text in the image. Scoring is VQA accuracy against human answers.

name: ThaiExam
description: Models answer multiple-choice questions from standardized examinations in Thailand, such as ONET, IC, TGAT, TPAT-1 and A-Level.

name: TheAgentCompany
description: Agents do work tasks in a simulated software company, using a browser, code, and chat with simulated coworkers. Scored by full and partial checkpoint completion.

name: TheoPhysEval
description: Agents solve 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems on their own, with literature search and scripts. Each final answer is checked against an expert answer, and the score is the pass rate.
org: ICTS Bengaluru (Suvrat Raju) with 35 researchers incl. Google DeepMind, Harvard and KU Leuven
note: Problems span 11 areas, from classical physics to holography. A realistic track allows web search and an isolated track does not. GPT-6 Astra passed 49 of 50 with search. Some expert reference answers were found wrong.

name: TheoremQA
description: Models solve 800 university-level questions in math, physics, EE and CS, and finance that each need a specific theorem. Scored by answer accuracy.

name: ThinkFollow (Qwen)
description: Models hold multi-turn dialogues with randomly inserted think and no-think flags and must switch reasoning mode correctly.
note: In-house Qwen evaluation. The data is not public.

name: Thrive Holdings helpdesk ticket resolution benchmark
description: Agent investigates IT support requests, takes action and decides when to escalate to a technician. Scored by pass rate.
note: Item count not stated. Drawn from Thrive's IT services firms.

name: TIIF-Bench
description: Image models generate short and long images scored on overall image quality.
note: GLM-Image reports short and long overall scores in its official model card.

name: Time Horizon Index: KSP
description: Agents get five days to build and run a space program in Kerbal Space Program. The score is progress through 30 fixed missions.
note: Vals estimates a human needs 90 to 120 hours for the first 28 missions. The board had 13 models on 2026-10-07.

name: Time series forecasting task (Anthropic)
description: Agents solve a regression and time-series forecasting problem with known state-of-the-art results, in six variants.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: TimeLens-Bench
description: Models find the start and end time of a described event in a video. The benchmark re-annotates Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions and QVHighlights with strict quality rules, and scores by mean IoU.
org: Nanjing University, ARC Lab (Tencent PCG) and Shanghai AI Lab
note: The authors report large model re-rankings compared with the original grounding benchmarks. Labs report the three subsets separately.

name: TimeSpeak
description: Models initiate speech at specified times while producing the requested content.
note: The launch post reports macro-averaged accuracy on an internal benchmark.

name: TIR-Bench
description: Models solve 13 kinds of image tasks that need tool use on images, such as rotation, jigsaw, and maze. Most items are multiple choice.
note: Qwen cards list two numbers for it, and the cards do not say which setting each one uses.

name: Toloka Arena
description: Agents handle private simulated enterprise workflows with live databases, API tools and strict business rules across nine domains. The main metric pass^5 needs all five trials to succeed.
note: Modeled on the tau-bench method. Launch post dated 2026-04-16.

name: TOMATO
description: Models answer 1,484 human-written questions about 1,417 videos that need visual temporal reasoning, such as action counts, direction, rotation and velocity. Scored by accuracy.
org: Yale University and Allen Institute for AI
note: Published at ICLR 2025. At release the best model trailed humans by 57.3 points.

name: TOMG-Bench
description: Models generate molecules from natural language requests in three tasks: molecule editing, molecule optimization and customized generation. Each output is checked for validity and for meeting the requested properties.
org: Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Shanghai AI Lab (Jiatong Li et al.)
note: The paper was later retitled Speak-to-Structure (S^2-Bench).

name: Tone
description: An automated evaluation measures whether model refusals are objective, neutral and not preachy.
note: In-house Google DeepMind evaluation. Model cards report only the change against an earlier Gemini model.

name: Tool use prompt injection evaluation (Anthropic)
description: Agents run bash commands where files, scripts or command outputs carry injected instructions. Score is the attack prevention rate.
note: In-house Anthropic evaluation reported without safeguards. The test cases are not public.

name: Tool-calling prompt injections
description: Agents receive prompt injections inside tool call outputs such as connectors. Scored on resisting the injected instructions.
note: In-house OpenAI evaluation. The tasks are not public.

name: Toolathlon
description: 108 long-horizon tasks across 32 apps through about 600 MCP tools. Execution-based checkers inspect final environment state.
note: Verified final release 2026-06-30. Do not mix with original-version scores.

name: Toolathlon-Verified
description: 108 long-horizon tasks across 32 apps through about 600 MCP tools. Execution-based checkers inspect final environment state.
note: A checked subset of Toolathlon tasks.

name: ToolBench
description: Models plan and call real REST APIs from RapidAPI, over 16,000 of them, to answer instructions that need one or many tools. ToolEval judges pass rate and win rate.
note: Released with the ToolLLM paper. Test groups G1, G2 and G3 differ in how many tools and categories a task spans. StableToolBench is a later stabilized variant.

name: ToolCall-Badcase
description: Models choose a tool and its arguments for 200 cases drawn from real user failure reports. Each case has a ground-truth call.
note: In-house Z.ai evaluation. The cases are not public.

name: ToolcallFormatIFBench
description: Models make tool calls that must follow format rules across many agent scaffolds and tool sets. Qwen uses it to measure real-world tool call following.
note: In-house. Defined in one footnote of the Qwen3.6-Max-Preview post.

name: ToolComp
description: Models chain several tool calls to answer 485 human-verified prompts. Most final answers are numbers. ToolComp-Enterprise gives 11 tools and ToolComp-Chat targets general chat tool use. Step labels also support process reward model tests.
note: Scale runs the two subsets as the Agentic Tool Use (Enterprise) and Agentic Tool Use (Chat) boards. The prompts carry 1,731 step-level labels. No public dataset was found.

name: ToolQA
description: Models answer questions that need outside information, using 13 tools such as database queries, text retrieval and a calculator over fixed data sources. The questions are built so that a model's internal knowledge cannot answer them. An easy and a hard set separate single lookups from multi-step tool use, and answers are checked by exact match.
note: About 290 GitHub stars, and the repo was last pushed in 2023-08.

name: ToolSandbox
description: Models use stateful tools in multi-turn conversations with a simulated user. Tools have hidden state dependencies, and runs are scored against milestones.
note: The repo moved to the apple-aiml-research organization on GitHub.

name: ToolUse (Qwen)
description: Models make single-turn, multi-turn and multi-step tool calls. The score combines intent recognition, format and parameter accuracy.
note: In-house Qwen evaluation. The data is not public.

name: ToRR
description: Models answer questions over tables given in several formats, and the board checks how much accuracy changes when the table format or prompt changes.
note: 10 datasets across table formats and domains. One HELM release, v1.0.0, on 2025-03-04.

name: ToxiGen
description: Models continue ToxiGen prompts about 13 minority groups. Scored by the average toxicity of the generations.
note: Generation use of ToxiGen. The classification use is toxigen-discriminative.

name: ToxiGen (discriminative)
description: Models label statements about 13 minority groups as toxic or neutral. Scored by accuracy, often split into toxic and neutral labels.
